questions.prompt: According to Lesson 1, which pair of consonants is pronounced the same?
choices: ב and פ, two distinctly different sounds
ג and כ, entirely separate sounds
ד and צ, not pronounced alike at all
ח and כ (no dagesh) — the same sound
questions.explanation: The book lists several look-different, sound-alike consonant pairs: א/ע (silent), ב/ו (v), ח/כ (ch as in BaCH), ט/ת (t), כ/ק (k), and ס/שׂ (s).

questions.prompt: Which of these consonants does NOT have a special final form?
questions.explanation: Only five letters change shape at the end of a word: כמנפצ become ךםןףץ. ת keeps one shape everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which four consonants does Lesson 1 group together as the "gutturals"?
questions.explanation: The gutturals — consonants pronounced in the back of the throat — are א, ח, ע, and ה.

questions.prompt: For which three letters does the presence or absence of the dot actually change how the letter sounds, per Lesson 1?
questions.explanation: Of the six בגדכפ״ת letters, only ב, כ, and פ audibly change sound with or without the dot (b/v, k/ch, p/f); ג, ד, ת are described as unchanged in this book's pronunciation scheme.

questions.prompt: Which Hebrew vowel sign is pronounced like the e in "Met"?
questions.explanation: סְגוֹל is the vowel sign given the value "e in Met" in the Lesson 2 chart.

questions.prompt: Two vowels both sound like "u" in Rude. Which one is written as a ו with a dot inside it, not as dots under the consonant?
questions.explanation: שׁוּרֶק is a vav carrying a dot; קִבּוּץ instead is three diagonal dots placed under the consonant, though both are pronounced [u].

questions.prompt: Where does a Hebrew vowel sign appear relative to its consonant, per Lesson 2?
choices: Always above the consonant, and never anywhere else
Under, over, or after the consonant it follows
Always to the left of the consonant, and never above or below it
Only inside a final-form letter, and nowhere else in the word
questions.explanation: Vowel signs are written under, over, or (for vowel letters like ה, ו, י) following the consonant they are pronounced after; no single position covers every vowel sign.

questions.prompt: True or False: Lesson 2 says that, unless told otherwise, you should read קָמֶץ as [a] (as in "father").
questions.explanation: קָמֶץ most often says [a]; the book tells students to default to [a] and learn to spot the rarer [o] value with experience.

questions.prompt: In which position is a שְׁוָא pronounced as vocal (a hurried "a" sound), per Lesson 3?
choices: When it follows a long vowel
When it is the first of two consecutive shevas
When it stands at the end of a syllable
When it stands at the very beginning of a word
questions.explanation: A שְׁוָא is vocal at the start of a word and as the second of two consecutive shevas; elsewhere it is silent.

questions.prompt: Which type of שְׁוָא appears under the guttural consonants to give them a fuller sound?
questions.explanation: Under gutturals, a plain vocal שְׁוָא is often replaced by a חֲטַף שְׁוָא, a compound sign combining שְׁוָא with one of the three basic vowels.

questions.prompt: Which Lesson 3 word is the divine name, traditionally read as unpronounceable as printed?
questions.explanation: יהוה is glossed in the vocabulary as "YHWH," the divine name that is unpronounceable as printed.

questions.prompt: In אֲדֹנָי the sign under א is חֲטַף פַּתַח rather than a plain vocal שְׁוָא. Why?
choices: Because א is a guttural consonant, which prefers a חֲטַף vowel
Because א belongs to the בגדכפ״ת consonant group
Because the שְׁוָא here is silent, not vocal
Because א always takes a full קָמֶץ vowel
questions.explanation: Gutturals like א typically take a חֲטַף sign instead of a plain vocal שְׁוָא, giving them a fuller, more audible sound.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between דָּגֵשׁ קַל and דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק, per Lesson 4?
choices: קל occurs only in the four guttural consonants, nowhere else
קל lengthens the consonant; חזק changes its pronunciation
they are simply the same dot, with no functional difference between them
קל affects a בגדכפ״ת letter's sound; חזק doubles most other consonants
questions.explanation: דָּגֵשׁ קַל appears in a בגדכפ״ת letter and switches it between a stop and a fricative sound, while דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק can occur in almost any consonant and lengthens/doubles it.

questions.prompt: A דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק can occur in any Hebrew consonant except which ones?
questions.explanation: Lesson 4 states that דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק can occur in any consonant except the gutturals and ר.

questions.prompt: In הַבֵּן [hab-ben], what does the dot in the ב indicate?
choices: A דָּגֵשׁ קַל, switching ב from fricative to stop without doubling it
A דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק, doubling the ב and forcing the stop sound
A חָטֵף פַתַח, a reduced vowel used under guttural letters
A missing final form, changing how ב is written
questions.explanation: The dot is a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק: it both doubles/lengthens the ב and, because ב is a בגדכפ״ת letter, forces its stop pronunciation.

questions.prompt: True or False: A דָּגֵשׁ קַל usually appears in a בגדכפ״ת letter only when a vowel or vocal שְׁוָא does not immediately precede it.
questions.explanation: Lesson 4 states that a דָּגֵשׁ קַל usually appears in a בגדכפ״ת letter precisely where there is no preceding vowel or vocal שְׁוָא.

questions.prompt: A dot inside ד could be a דָּגֵשׁ קַל or a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק. Based on Lessons 1 and 4, what distinguishes their effect on ד?
choices: קל makes no audible difference to ד; חָזָק lengthens/doubles it
קל lengthens/doubles ד; חָזָק makes no audible difference to it
קל and חָזָק both always double the consonant
קל occurs only in guttural consonants; חָזָק never does
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 states only ב, כ, and פ switch sound with a דָּגֵשׁ קַל; ג, ד, and ת sound the same with or without it. A דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק, by contrast, always lengthens/doubles the consonant it marks, per Lesson 4.

questions.prompt: Reading אֲנִי aloud, what kind of שְׁוָא sits under א, and why?
choices: A silent שְׁוָא, because it follows a short vowel
A plain vocal שְׁוָא, because א is not a guttural
A חֲטַף פַּתַח, because א is a guttural consonant
A דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק, because gutturals double consonants
questions.explanation: Because א is one of the four gutturals, it takes a חֲטַף vowel instead of a plain vocal שְׁוָא, giving אֲנִי its chatef-patach.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Hebrew letter/vowel homophony (Lessons 1-2) is correct?
choices: א and ה sound identical; קָמֶץ and צֵרֶי sound identical
א and ע sound identical; קָמֶץ and פַּתָח can both say [a]
ת and שׁ sound identical; חִירֶק and סְגוֹל sound identical
ר and ל sound identical; שׁוּרֶק and חוֹלֶם sound identical
questions.explanation: א and ע are both silent/glottal in this book's pronunciation, and both קָמֶץ and פַּתָח can represent the [a] sound.

questions.prompt: Following the pattern אֲנִי יוֹסֵף, which phrase best fits "I am [the] LORD"?
questions.explanation: אֲנִי is the 1cs pronoun "I"; placed before a noun it yields "I am [noun]," matching the book's own אֲנִי יוֹסֵף pattern.

questions.prompt: הַבֵּן is pronounced [hab-ben] with a doubled ב, even though ב alone would be a fricative [v]. Which rule explains this?
choices: The vocal-שְׁוָא rule, which supplies a helping vowel before consonant clusters
The guttural chatef-vowel rule, which reduces vowels under guttural letters
The final-form rule, which changes a letter's shape at the end of a word
A דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק in ב, which doubles it and forces the stop sound
questions.explanation: The doubling dot is a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק; since ב is a בגדכפ״ת letter, that same dot also forces its stop pronunciation.

questions.prompt: The word מִדְבָּר has a silent שְׁוָא under ד. Why is it silent rather than vocal?
choices: Because ד is one of the guttural consonants
Because it is the first of two consecutive shevas
Because it is not word-initial or the second sheva
Because the מ before it carries a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק
questions.explanation: A שְׁוָא is vocal only at the start of a word or as the second of two consecutive shevas; everywhere else, including here, it is silent.

questions.prompt: Which two Lesson 5 pronouns are distinguished from each other only by a final ה, both meaning "you" but differing in the addressee's gender?
questions.explanation: אַתָּה ("you," ms) adds a final ה that אַתְּ ("you," fs) lacks; both mean "you" but differ by the addressee's gender.

questions.prompt: True or False: Lesson 3 says a שְׁוָא under a guttural is always fully silent and is never modified.
questions.explanation: False — under gutturals a vocal שְׁוָא is often replaced by a חֲטַף sign instead, as in אֲדֹנָי.

questions.prompt: What is the "default" reading this book gives for קָמֶץ if you have no other information?
choices: סְגוֹל, the e in Met vowel
חִירֶק, the i in Machine vowel
שׁוּרֶק, the u in Rude vowel
questions.explanation: Unless told otherwise, the book instructs students to read קָמֶץ as [a], reserving the rarer [o] value for cases learned by experience.

questions.prompt: Reading אַתָּה aloud, the doubled ת reflects which Lesson 4 rule, given that ת is not a guttural or ר?
choices: A דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק, which cannot occur in gutturals or ר, cannot occur in ת either
A דָּגֵשׁ קַל, which only affects ב, כ, and פ's pronunciation
A דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק, which can double any consonant except gutturals and ר
A general rule that ת always doubles, with or without any דָּגֵשׁ
questions.explanation: Since ת is neither a guttural nor ר, it is eligible for a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק, which is exactly what lengthens it in אַתָּה.

questions.prompt: Which independent subject pronoun means "she" (3fs)?
questions.explanation: הִיא is the 3fs independent subject pronoun, "she."

questions.prompt: Which pair of pronouns share the same consonants and differ mainly by a final ה marking gender (2ms vs. 2fs)?
questions.explanation: אַתָּה ("you," ms) and אַתְּ ("you," fs) are the singular second-person pronouns, distinguished mainly by the final ה.

questions.prompt: Following the book's own pattern אֲנִי יוֹסֵף ("I am Joseph"), which phrase correctly says "He is God"?
questions.explanation: הוּא ("he") is the 3ms pronoun; placed before a noun with no copula verb, it yields "he is [noun]," here "He is God."

questions.prompt: If you are speaking directly to a woman, which Lesson 5 pronoun for "you" should you use?
questions.explanation: אַתְּ is the 2fs form, used to address a female conversation partner directly.

questions.prompt: Lesson 6 gives three ways to express the "to be" copula in a clause. Which of these is NOT one of them?
choices: Omitting the copula entirely and letting context show tense
Using a third-person pronoun as a substitute copula
Doubling the subject noun for emphasis
questions.explanation: The three methods given are an omitted copula, the verb הָיָה, and a third-person independent pronoun used as a substitute copula. Doubling a noun is not a copula strategy in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Which form of הָיָה ("was") agrees with a 3fs ("she") subject?
questions.explanation: הָיְתָה is the 3fs form, "she was"; הָיָה is 3ms, and the other two forms are not part of this lesson's paradigm.

questions.prompt: Which Hebrew sentence correctly means "Who was a lord?" using the verbal copula?
questions.explanation: מִי ("who?") plus the 3ms verb הָיָה plus the predicate noun אָדוֹן gives "Who was a lord?"; the other options are either scrambled, declarative, or negated.

questions.prompt: In חָם הוּא אֲבִי כְנָעַן ("Ham is the father of Canaan"), which copula strategy is being used?
choices: A third-person pronoun as a substitute copula
The omitted-copula strategy, with no copula word at all
The verb הָיָה used explicitly as the copula
The definite article attached to the noun
questions.explanation: הוּא here does not mean a separate "he"; it functions as a substitute "is," linking the subject to its predicate.

questions.prompt: How is a masculine singular noun typically marked, per Lesson 7?
choices: By adding a ה, following the pattern of many feminine nouns
By adding a ת, as a smaller class of feminine nouns does
By adding a וּ, matching a plural verb ending instead
By adding nothing — the masculine singular stays bare
questions.explanation: Masculine singular nouns have no inflectional ending; feminine singular nouns often add ־ה or, less often, ־ת.

questions.prompt: Which Lesson 7 noun is feminine despite having no overt feminine ending?
questions.explanation: אֵם ("mother") is feminine but carries no ה־ or ת־ marker, unlike אֲדָמָה and בְּרִית, which are feminine with overt endings; אָח ("brother") is simply masculine, so it is not a counterexample at all.

questions.prompt: Which Hebrew sentence correctly means "The daughter was female" (bare nouns, no article)?
questions.explanation: בַּת (fs subject) needs the matching fs verb הָיְתָה and the predicate נְקֵבָה ("female"); the distractors mismatch the subject noun, scramble the word order, or mismatch the predicate's meaning.

questions.prompt: What is the correct feminine singular form of the paradigm noun סוּס ("stallion"), per Lesson 7?
questions.explanation: The feminine singular is formed by adding ־ָה: סוּסָה, "mare."

questions.prompt: How does Lesson 8 distinguish the definite article from the interrogative ה, since they look alike?
choices: The article is used only with proper nouns
The article marks a question; the interrogative marks a noun as definite
They are the same particle with identical meaning
The article marks a noun definite; the interrogative marks a yes/no question
questions.explanation: The article (ה plus דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק) makes a noun definite, "the," while the interrogative ה prefixed to a clause marks it as a yes/no question.

questions.prompt: What happens to the noun immediately after the definite article, per Lesson 8?
choices: Its final consonant gets a final form
Its first consonant takes a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק
Its vowels are replaced with שְׁוָא
questions.explanation: The article's form is ה plus a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק placed in the noun's first consonant, as in מִדְבָּר becoming הַמִּדְבָּר, "the wilderness."

questions.prompt: Which Lesson 8 word means "house," with irregular plural בָּתִּים?
questions.explanation: בַּיִת, "house," has the irregular plural בָּתִּים given in the Lesson 8 vocabulary.

questions.prompt: In הֲשָׁלוֹם לוֹ, what does the initial הֲ indicate?
choices: That the clause is a yes/no question
questions.explanation: The interrogative ה here marks the whole clause as a yes/no question, "Is there peace to him?" (i.e., "Is he well?").

questions.prompt: Which form of ל plus pronoun means "belongs to her / hers," per Lesson 9?
questions.explanation: לָהּ is ל plus the 3fs suffix, "belongs to her."

questions.prompt: What happens to the definite article's ה when ל attaches to a noun that already has the article?
choices: The article's vowel disappears entirely, leaving only ל
Nothing changes at all; both ה and ל simply appear together
The ה is replaced by ל, and the article's vocalization is kept
The noun instead loses its final consonant entirely
questions.explanation: The vocalization of the article is retained, but its ה is replaced by the attached ל, as in לַיֶּלֶד ("to the child").

questions.prompt: Which phrase correctly means "The king had land" ("To the king was land")?
questions.explanation: אֶרֶץ is feminine and is the grammatical subject, so it takes the fs verb הָיְתָה, and לַמֶּלֶךְ fuses the article with ל for "to the king."

questions.prompt: How does Lesson 9 explain the sense of לְלוֹט הָיָה צֹאן... ("To Lot were sheep...")?
choices: It is equivalent to English "Lot had sheep"
It means that Lot himself was a shepherd
It marks Lot as the sentence's direct object
It is a yes/no question asked about Lot
questions.explanation: ל plus a copular clause expresses possession; the literal "to Lot were sheep" corresponds to English "Lot had sheep."

questions.prompt: Compare הוּא אֲדֹנָי ("he is Lord", pronoun-copula) with לוֹ אָדוֹן ("he has a lord", ל-possession). What is the key structural difference?
choices: They mean exactly the same thing, since both sentences are simple copulas
The first uses הוּא as a copula meaning "is"; the second uses לוֹ, a preposition marking possession
The first uses the definite article on אֲדֹנָי; the second lacks any article at all
The second is a yes-no question about lordship; the first is a plain declarative statement
questions.explanation: In the first sentence, הוּא substitutes for "is" to link subject and predicate; in the second, לוֹ is ל plus a pronoun suffix expressing possession, a different construction entirely.

questions.prompt: אֹזֶן ("ear") is feminine with no overt feminine ending, like the paired body parts in Lesson 7. What is its dual form?
questions.explanation: אֹזֶן takes the dual ending ־ַיִם, giving אָזְנַיִם, "ears," consistent with its status as a naturally-paired body part.

questions.prompt: Which phrase correctly means "The king had a hand" (i.e., "To the king was a hand")?
questions.explanation: יָד is feminine singular, so it needs the fs verb הָיְתָה, and "the king" requires the article fused with ל as לַמֶּלֶךְ, not the bare לְמֶלֶךְ.

questions.prompt: בַּיִת becomes הַבַּיִת with the article, and its plural is בָּתִּים. What happens if the article is added to the plural?
choices: The ה is dropped entirely once the noun is already plural
The plural ending ־ִים changes to ־וֹת once the article attaches
The article's ה plus דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק simply prefixes the plural noun
The noun needs an entirely new triconsonantal root
questions.explanation: The article works the same way on the plural as on the singular: ה plus דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק prefixed to the noun, here הַבָּתִּים, "the houses."

questions.prompt: Which declarative sentence illustrates the Lesson 6 omitted-copula strategy while also using the Lesson 8 definite article?
questions.explanation: הָאִישׁ אָב ("the man [is] a father") is declarative and has no copula word at all — the article makes the subject definite, and context supplies "is." הָאִישׁ הָיָה אָב uses the explicit verbal copula הָיָה; הוּא הָאִישׁ uses the pronoun-as-copula strategy instead; and מִי הָאִישׁ is a question, not a declarative clause.

questions.prompt: Lesson 9's ל plus pronoun set (e.g. לִי, "to/for me") parallels which set of forms from Lesson 5?
choices: The independent subject pronouns, sharing the same person/gender/number categories
The plural noun endings, sharing the same singular/plural categories
The interrogative ה, sharing the same yes/no question category
The דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק rule, sharing the same doubling/lengthening category
questions.explanation: The ל-of-possession suffixes track the same person, gender, and number categories as the independent subject pronouns (3ms, 3fs, 2ms, 2fs, 1cs).

questions.prompt: Both אִשָּׁה ("woman") and אָב ("father") have irregular plurals. Which pair correctly matches each singular to its irregular plural?
questions.explanation: אָב irregularly pluralizes to אָבוֹת, and אִשָּׁה suppletes to the unrelated-looking נָשִׁים; בָּנִים is instead the plural of בֵּן, "son."

questions.prompt: Which is the correctly articled plural of בַּיִת ("house"; plural בָּתִּים)?
questions.explanation: The article ה plus דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק attaches to the plural noun בָּתִּים the same way it does to any singular noun, giving הַבָּתִּים, "the houses."

questions.prompt: Out of context, what does לוֹ אִשָּׁה most likely mean, applying the Lesson 9 ל-possession pattern?
choices: "He is a woman", misapplying the pronoun-copula pattern
"He has a wife", using ל-possession rather than a pronoun copula
"Is he a woman?", misreading לוֹ as the interrogative ה
"The woman is his", assuming an article that isn't present
questions.explanation: לוֹ אִשָּׁה follows the ל-possession pattern from Lesson 9 ("to him [is] a woman"), which corresponds to English "he has a wife."

questions.prompt: הַנַּעֲרָה ("the young woman") has a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק in נ from the article and a final ה that is not the article. What explains that final ה?
choices: The article's ה attaches at the front; the final ה is the unrelated feminine ending
Both ה's are the same article, simply repeated for emphasis
The final ה is purely silent, with no grammatical function at all
The final ה marks the noun as plural, like the ־וֹת ending
questions.explanation: The article (ה plus דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק) prefixes the noun, while the final ה is the separate feminine singular ending; the two ה's serve unrelated functions.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct dual form of יָד ("hand"), per Lesson 10?
questions.explanation: The dual ending ־ַיִם gives יָדַיִם, "hands," for this naturally-paired body part.

questions.prompt: Lesson 10 says the dual is largely confined to which category of nouns?
choices: Abstract nouns, like ideas or virtues
Nouns for divine or heavenly beings
Things that occur naturally in pairs
Proper names of cities or nations
questions.explanation: The dual is mostly used for naturally-paired items such as eyes, hands, and feet.

questions.prompt: What is the irregular plural of אִישׁ ("man"), per Lesson 10?
questions.explanation: אִישׁ has the suppletive irregular plural אֲנָשִׁים, "men," which must be memorized.

questions.prompt: True or False: Lesson 10 says the dual ending is used for all plural nouns in Hebrew, not just naturally-paired items.
questions.explanation: False — general plurality uses ־ים or ־ות; the dual is reserved for things that occur naturally in pairs.

questions.prompt: Which independent pronoun means 'they' (feminine plural)?
questions.explanation: הֵן is the 3fp independent pronoun 'they' (feminine). הֵם is masculine plural, אַתֶּן is 2fp 'you', and אֲנַחְנוּ is 1cp 'we'.

questions.prompt: Which third-person pronominal copula correctly completes כָּל־הַנָּשִׁים ____ אִמּוֹת ('all the women are mothers')?
questions.explanation: הַנָּשִׁים ('the women') is feminine plural, so the copula must agree as 3fp הֵן. הֵם is masculine plural, and הוּא/הִיא are singular.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ____ עֲבָדִים ('We are servants').
questions.explanation: 'We' is the 1cp independent pronoun אֲנַחְנוּ. אֲנִי is 1cs 'I', אַתֶּם is 2mp 'you', and הֵם is 3mp 'they'.

questions.prompt: Which spelling of 'all/every' is used when it is attached to the following word with a מַקֵּף?
questions.explanation: The maqqef-attached form is כָּל־, written with a qamats rather than the standalone form's cholam (כֹּל).

questions.prompt: Which particle serves as the negative existential copula, meaning 'is/are not, there is/are not'?
questions.explanation: אֵין is the negative existential copula. יֵשׁ is its positive counterpart, לֹא is the general negative particle, and מָקוֹם means 'place'.

questions.prompt: How would יֵשׁ לִי מָקוֹם best be translated?
choices: There is no place for me.
questions.explanation: יֵשׁ combined with the ל of possession attached to a pronoun expresses 'have', so יֵשׁ לִי מָקוֹם literally 'a place is to me' means 'I have a place'.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the sentence means 'There is no king there': אֵין מֶלֶךְ ____.
questions.explanation: שָׁם is the adverb 'there'. מָקוֹם means 'place' (a noun, not 'there'), שָׁלוֹם means 'peace', and כֹּל means 'all'.

questions.prompt: True or False: יֵשׁ and אֵין can both function as copulas, meaning 'is/are' and 'is/are not' respectively.
questions.explanation: Both words are grammatical copulas: יֵשׁ asserts existence ('is/are') and אֵין negates it ('is/are not').

questions.prompt: Which preposition means 'like, as'?
questions.explanation: כְּ means 'like, as'. בְּ means 'in, at', לְ means 'to, for', and מִן means 'from, out of, more than'.

questions.prompt: When מִן attaches to a following word that begins with a non-guttural consonant, what happens?
choices: מִן stays a fully separate, unattached word
The נ of מִן simply drops, with no compensation at all
מִן is written as מ plus a dagesh doubling the following consonant
The following consonant instead becomes completely silent
questions.explanation: The final נ of מִן assimilates into the next consonant, which then takes a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק, as in מִשָּׁם (מִן + שָׁם).

questions.prompt: Which form results from combining מִן with אֶרֶץ ('from a land')?
questions.explanation: Because אֶרֶץ begins with a guttural, מִן attaches as מ with no dagesh, giving מֵאֶרֶץ rather than a doubled consonant.

questions.prompt: In הַמֶּלֶךְ וְהָעֶבֶד ('the king and the servant'), what role does the וְ play?
choices: It marks the start of a new clause
questions.explanation: Here the וְ conjunction performs its first function, joining two words together; its other function is to mark the start of a new clause without needing translation.

questions.prompt: Which interrogative asks 'how much? how many?'
questions.explanation: כַּמָּה means 'how much/how many?'. מָתַי asks 'when?', אֵיפֹה asks 'where?', and לָמָּה asks 'why?'.

questions.prompt: Which interrogative means 'to where?'
questions.explanation: אָנָה means 'where? to where?'. מֵאַיִן means 'from where?', אֵיפֹה means 'where?', and מָתַי means 'when?'.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the sentence means 'Where is the king?': ____ הַמֶּלֶךְ?
questions.explanation: אֵיפֹה is one of the interrogatives meaning 'where?'. מָה asks 'what?', מִי asks 'who?', and לָמָּה asks 'why?'.

questions.prompt: לָמָּה and מַדּוּעַ both correspond to which English question word?
questions.explanation: לָמָּה and מַדּוּעַ are two alternate interrogatives both meaning 'why?'.

questions.prompt: Which pronoun would you use to say 'you' to a group of men (masculine plural)?
questions.explanation: אַתֶּם is the 2mp independent pronoun. אַתָּה is 2ms singular, אַתְּ is 2fs singular, and אַתֶּן is 2fp.

questions.prompt: עַם and עִם look similar but differ in Hebrew. Based on their vowel points, what is the difference in meaning?
choices: Both mean 'people'; they are spelling variants
Both mean 'with'; they are spelling variants
questions.explanation: עַם (with patach) means 'people' (introduced in Lesson 15); עִם (with chirik) is the preposition 'with' (already introduced in Lesson 13) — distinct words distinguished only by vocalization.

questions.prompt: Which best expresses 'She has a house' using יֵשׁ with the לְ of possession?
questions.explanation: 'She has' requires the 3fs possessive form לָהּ combined with the positive existential יֵשׁ, giving יֵשׁ לָהּ בַּיִת.

questions.prompt: Which type of question does the attached interrogative הֲ (as opposed to מִי or מָה) introduce?
questions.explanation: The attached הֲ marks a yes-no question, while dedicated question words like מִי, מָה, אֵיפֹה, and לָמָּה introduce open questions expecting specific circumstantial answers.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the sentence means 'The brothers are there': הָאַחִים ____ שָׁם.
questions.explanation: הָאַחִים (the irregular plural of אָח) is masculine plural, so the copula must be 3mp הֵם.

questions.prompt: When מִן attaches directly to a word beginning with a guttural consonant, what happens instead of gemination?
choices: The מ doubles the following consonant with a דָּגֵשׁ חָזָק
It stays a fully separate word, with no attachment at all
The מ is written with no דָּגֵשׁ following
questions.explanation: Gutturals cannot take a דָּגֵשׁ, so before a guttural-initial word מִן attaches as a bare מ with no doubling, as in מֵאִישׁ.

questions.prompt: A Hebrew dictionary typically lists verbs by which form?
questions.explanation: Hebrew verbs are conventionally listed in a lexicon by the 3ms Qal Perfect form, e.g. שָׁמַר 'he guarded'.

questions.prompt: Based on the aspectual overview in the verb preview, which best characterizes the קָטַל/Perfect conjugation's basic aspect?
questions.explanation: The קָטַל/Perfect has a 'whole view' perfective aspect and most often describes what occurred in the past.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the sentence means 'We [are] before the king': אֲנַחְנוּ ____ הַמֶּלֶךְ.
questions.explanation: לִפְנֵי means 'before'. עַל means 'upon, over', מִן means 'from', and עִם means 'with' — none fit this sense.

questions.prompt: True or False: The interrogative words מַדּוּעַ and לָמָּה both mean 'where?'
questions.explanation: מַדּוּעַ and לָמָּה both mean 'why?', not 'where?'; 'where?' is expressed instead by אַי/אַיֵּה/אֵיפֹה.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the three root consonants from which most Hebrew lexical words are derived?
questions.explanation: The שֹׁרֶשׁ is the triconsonantal root. בִּנְיָן names a verb construction pattern, and קָטַל/יִקְטֹל name Hebrew's two basic verb conjugations.

questions.prompt: How many primary בִּנְיָנִים does Biblical Hebrew have?
questions.explanation: Biblical Hebrew has seven primary בִּנְיָנִים, whose traditional names derive from the 3ms Perfect form of the root פ-ע-ל 'to do'.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the aspectual difference between קָטַל (Perfect) and יִקְטֹל?
choices: קָטַל portrays an action in progress; יִקְטֹל portrays it as complete
קָטַל portrays an action as a whole; יִקְטֹל portrays it as partial/in progress
both portray actions identically but differ only in gender
קָטַל is used for questions; יִקְטֹל is used for statements
questions.explanation: The קָטַל (Perfect) has a 'whole view' (perfective) aspect, usually with past-time reference, while יִקְטֹל has a 'partial/in-progress view' (imperfective) aspect, usually with non-past reference.

questions.prompt: Because the meaning relationships among בִּנְיָנִים are not consistent, what follows for how a student should learn a verb's meaning?
choices: The meaning of each verb in its בִּנְיָן must be memorized individually
The meaning can always be derived automatically from the קַל form
Only the שֹׁרֶשׁ determines meaning, regardless of בִּנְיָן
Such patterns never change a verb's basic meaning
questions.explanation: Since a שֹׁרֶשׁ's meaning is not predictable across בִּנְיָנִים, each verb's meaning within a given בִּנְיָן has to be learned on its own.

questions.prompt: Which Qal Perfect form means 'you (ms) guarded'?
questions.explanation: שָׁמַרְתָּ is the 2ms Qal Perfect form. שָׁמַר is 3ms, שָׁמְרָה is 3fs, and שָׁמְרוּ is 3cp.

questions.prompt: In the Qal Perfect, the ending תִּי- marks which person, gender, and number?
questions.explanation: The 1cs Qal Perfect suffix is תִּי-, as in שָׁמַרְתִּי "I guarded"; it is unique to first-person singular and is not shared by any other person/gender/number in the paradigm.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the sentence means 'You (fs) guarded the way': אַתְּ ____ אֶת־הַדֶּרֶךְ.
questions.explanation: שָׁמַרְתְּ is the 2fs Qal Perfect form, matching the subject אַתְּ. שָׁמַר is 3ms, שָׁמְרָה is 3fs, and שְׁמַרְתֶּם is 2mp.

questions.prompt: The Qal Perfect 3fs of הָיָה is הָיְתָה rather than a fully regular form. What does this illustrate?
choices: An irregular verb form that must be memorized alongside the regular paradigm
A completely regular application of the שָׁמַר paradigm, with no exception
A form that only appears outside the Perfect paradigm entirely
A form that never, under any circumstance, occurs in the Perfect paradigm
questions.explanation: הָיָה is both frequent and irregular, so its Perfect paradigm must be learned individually alongside the regular שָׁמַר pattern.

questions.prompt: Which form means 'we have / to us'?
questions.explanation: לָנוּ is לְ plus the 1cp suffix, meaning 'we have / to us'. לָכֶם is 2mp, and לָהֶם/לָהֶן are 3mp/3fp.

questions.prompt: Which form means 'they have' (masculine plural)?
questions.explanation: לָהֶם is לְ plus the 3mp suffix, 'they have / to them (m)'. לָכֶם/לָכֶן are 2mp/2fp, and לָנוּ is 1cp.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the sentence means 'The man gave the men bread': הָאִישׁ נָתַן ____ לֶחֶם.
questions.explanation: לָהֶם is the 3mp form, 'to/for the men.' לָנוּ means 'to us', לָהֶן is 3fp ('to the women'), and לָכֶם is 2mp ('to you all').

questions.prompt: In a non-copular clause like נָתַן־לִי לֶחֶם ('He gave to me bread'), how does the לְ + pronoun construction function grammatically?
choices: As an ordinary prepositional phrase ('to/for' + pronoun)
As the main grammatical subject governing the clause
As a possessive copula construction meaning 'I have'
As a direct object marker attached before the verb
questions.explanation: Outside the possessive-copula use, לְ with an attached pronoun works as a simple prepositional phrase indicating the recipient, 'to/for' someone.

questions.prompt: What is the basic word order of a Hebrew clause with an overt subject and verb?
questions.explanation: Like English, the basic order of a Hebrew clause is Subject-Verb, though Hebrew frequently inverts to Verb-Subject in certain conditions.

questions.prompt: Which of these commonly triggers inversion to Verb-Subject order?
questions.explanation: Relatives like אֲשֶׁר and שֶׁ, interrogatives, negatives, and most other clause-initial grammatical words trigger inversion, but the וְ conjunction and עַתָּה notably do not.

questions.prompt: In the clause כַּאֲשֶׁר יָשַׁב הַמֶּלֶךְ ('when the king sat'), what word order appears after כַּאֲשֶׁר?
questions.explanation: כַּאֲשֶׁר is one of the grammatical words that triggers inversion, so the verb יָשַׁב precedes its subject הַמֶּלֶךְ.

questions.prompt: True or False: The וְ conjunction and עַתָּה ('now') are among the few grammatical words that do NOT generally trigger Verb-Subject inversion.
questions.explanation: Unlike אֲשֶׁר, כִּי, interrogatives, and negatives, the וְ conjunction and עַתָּה are exceptions that do not generally trigger the inverted order.

questions.prompt: Which Qal Perfect form means 'you all (mp) guarded'?
questions.explanation: שְׁמַרְתֶּם is the 2mp Qal Perfect form. שָׁמְרוּ is 3cp, שָׁמַרְנוּ is 1cp, and שָׁמַרְתִּי is 1cs.

questions.prompt: In the Qal Perfect, the ending וּ- marks which person, gender, and number?
questions.explanation: The 3cp Qal Perfect suffix is וּ-, as in שָׁמְרוּ "they guarded". תֶּם-/תֶּן- mark 2mp/2fp, and נוּ- marks 1cp.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the sentence means 'We heard the voice': אֲנַחְנוּ ____ אֶת־הַקּוֹל.
questions.explanation: שָׁמַעְנוּ is the 1cp Qal Perfect of שָׁמַע, matching the subject אֲנַחְנוּ. שְׁמַעְתֶּם is 2mp, שָׁמְעוּ is 3cp, and שָׁמַע is 3ms.

questions.prompt: In the 3rd person plural of the Qal Perfect (e.g. שָׁמְרוּ 'they guarded'), how is gender distinguished between masculine and feminine subjects?
choices: It isn't — the 3cp form is common gender and used for both
By using a noticeably different vowel pattern for feminine
By adding a special ן- ending exclusively for feminine
By dropping the final וּ ending entirely for feminine
questions.explanation: Unlike the singular Perfect forms, the 3rd person plural Perfect has a single common-gender form, שָׁמְרוּ, used for both masculine and feminine subjects.

questions.prompt: Which Qal Perfect form of שָׁמַר means 'you all (fp) guarded'?
questions.explanation: שְׁמַרְתֶּן is the 2fp Qal Perfect form. שָׁמְרָה is 3fs singular, שָׁמַרְתְּ is 2fs singular, and שָׁמְרוּ is 3cp.

questions.prompt: According to the word-order patterns taught through Lesson 18, what is the default order of subject and verb when no clause-initial trigger word (like אֲשֶׁר or an interrogative) is present?
questions.explanation: The basic, untriggered order in Hebrew is Subject-Verb; Verb-Subject order becomes frequent specifically when a clause-initial element like a relative, interrogative, or negative precedes it.

questions.prompt: Which form of הָיָה means 'you all (mp) were'?
questions.explanation: הֱיִיתֶם is the 2mp Qal Perfect of הָיָה. הָיִיתָ is 2ms singular, הָיוּ is 3cp, and הָיִינוּ is 1cp.

questions.prompt: How would 'the words of the servant' be expressed using סְמִיכוּת with the plural of דָּבָר?
questions.explanation: The masculine plural construct form of דָּבָר is דִּבְרֵי, so 'the words of the servant' is דִּבְרֵי הָעֶבֶד.

questions.prompt: Since מִי is one of the interrogatives that triggers inversion, what word order would you expect in a clause beginning with מִי?
questions.explanation: Interrogatives are among the grammatical words that trigger inversion to Verb-Subject order.

questions.prompt: Which best translates יֵשׁ לָהֶם לֶחֶם?
questions.explanation: יֵשׁ combined with the 3mp possessive form לָהֶם expresses 'they have', so the phrase means 'they have bread'.

questions.prompt: In כִּי שָׁמְרוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים אֶת־הַדֶּרֶךְ ('because the men guarded the way'), what triggers the Verb-Subject word order here?
choices: The causal conjunction כִּי introducing the clause
The verb's own plural ending וּ-, marking the subject
The direct-object marker אֶת placed later in the clause
The plural noun הָאֲנָשִׁים functioning as subject
questions.explanation: כִּי is one of the grammatical words that triggers inversion, so the Qal Perfect verb שָׁמְרוּ precedes its subject הָאֲנָשִׁים.

questions.prompt: If נְבִיאֵי ('prophets of') is bound to the proper noun יְהוָה, why does the whole phrase mean 'the prophets of YHWH' (definite), even though נְבִיאֵי has no article?
choices: Because plural nouns are always definite by default
Because bound nouns take a special definite suffix marker
Because proper nouns can always be freely pluralized
Because the נִסְמָךְ inherits definiteness from the definite סוֹמֵךְ
questions.explanation: A נִסְמָךְ cannot itself take the article, but when its סוֹמֵךְ is a proper noun (inherently definite), the whole bound phrase counts as definite.

questions.prompt: Which of these expresses '(to) me' as opposed to '(to) us' using the לְ of possession?
questions.explanation: לִי is the 1cs form, 'to/for me'. לָנוּ is 1cp 'to us', לָכֶם is 2mp, and לָהֶם is 3mp.

questions.prompt: True or False: A Qal Perfect verb like שָׁמְרוּ ('they guarded') distinguishes masculine from feminine in the 3rd person plural, just as the singular forms do.
questions.explanation: The 3rd person plural of the Qal Perfect is common gender — a single form שָׁמְרוּ covers both masculine and feminine subjects, unlike the gender-marked singular forms.

questions.prompt: In the phrase דְּבַר־הָעֶבֶד ('the word of the servant'), which is the נִסְמָךְ ('bound/supported') word?
questions.explanation: The נִסְמָךְ is the first, bound word — here דְּבַר — while the following word (הָעֶבֶד) is the סוֹמֵךְ that supports it.

questions.prompt: What happens to the vowel pattern of דָּבָר ('word') when it takes construct/bound form before another noun?
questions.explanation: In the bound (construct) singular form, דָּבָר shortens to דְּבַר, since the two words in סְמִיכוּת are stressed as a single unit.

questions.prompt: A נִסְמָךְ noun such as the first word of a סְמִיכוּת phrase cannot itself take...
questions.explanation: A נִסְמָךְ noun cannot carry the definite article directly; if the phrase is definite, the נִסְמָךְ instead inherits definiteness from a definite סוֹמֵךְ.

questions.prompt: In נְבִיאֵי יְהוָה ('the prophets of YHWH'), why is נְבִיאֵי understood as definite even though it has no article?
choices: Because it inherits definiteness from the proper noun יְהוָה that follows it
Because all bound plural nouns are automatically definite in every case
Because prophets themselves are inherently a definite class of persons
Because the מַקֵּף hyphen alone makes any phrase fully definite
questions.explanation: When the סוֹמֵךְ noun is a proper noun (or has the article), the נִסְמָךְ inherits that definiteness, even without an article of its own.

questions.prompt: The Irreal (non-real) use of the Perfect conjugation is distinguished from its real, event-reporting use mainly by one grammatical signal. What is it?
choices: A negated verb marked somewhere with the negative particle לֹא
An attached pronoun suffix appearing directly on the verb itself
The definite article attached in front of the subject noun itself
Verb-Subject word order (instead of the real mood's Subject-Verb order)
questions.explanation: Real-mood Perfect clauses keep the basic Subject-Verb order, while Irreal Perfect clauses invert to Verb-Subject order; most Irreal Perfects are also prefixed with וְ, though word order is the defining signal.

questions.prompt: Read this clause: וְשָׁמְרָה הָאִשָּׁה אֶת־הַיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי — the verb שָׁמְרָה precedes its subject הָאִשָּׁה and is prefixed with וְ, and the sentence is being spoken as an instruction to her ('she must keep the seventh day'). Which function of the Irreal Perfect does this illustrate?
choices: A causal clause explaining a prior statement
An instruction or command imposed on a listener
questions.explanation: The Irreal Perfect marks instructions and commands imposed by a speaker on a listener; the inverted Verb-Subject order plus the וְ prefix signal that שָׁמְרָה here is not simply reporting that she kept the day, but instructing her to do so.

questions.prompt: Read this clause, understood from its surrounding context as describing something that used to happen again and again: וְהָלְכוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים בָּעִיר ('the men would go about in the city'). Which function of the Irreal Perfect does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: The Irreal Perfect also marks habitual events; the Verb-Subject order (הָלְכוּ before הָאֲנָשִׁים) with the וְ prefix signals a repeated pattern of action rather than a single completed event.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly converts the real-mood clause הָאִישׁ שָׁמַר אֶת־הַיּוֹם (Subject-Verb order: 'the man kept the day') into an Irreal Perfect clause expressing a command?
questions.explanation: Converting to the Irreal Perfect requires inverting to Verb-Subject order and prefixing the verb with וְ, giving וְשָׁמַר הָאִישׁ אֶת־הַיּוֹם; simply moving the וְ elsewhere in the clause does not create the irreal word order.

questions.prompt: בְּרִיתִי is built by attaching a pronoun suffix to the construct form of בְּרִית ('covenant'). Which pronoun does this suffix express?
questions.explanation: The ־ִי ending is the 1cs attached-pronoun suffix, so בְּרִיתִי means 'my covenant'; because בְּרִית already ends in ת, the suffix attaches directly with no further change to the noun's ending.

questions.prompt: An attached pronoun makes a noun definite, and a definite noun cannot also take the article הַ. Given the paradigm noun דָּבָר ('word'), which of these is therefore ungrammatical?
questions.explanation: Because an attached pronoun already makes the noun definite, combining it with the article as in הַדְּבָרִי is not permitted; a noun is either הַדָּבָר or דְּבָרִי, never both.

questions.prompt: בְּרִיתְךָ ('your covenant') attaches a pronoun suffix to the construct form of בְּרִית. Which person, gender, and number does this suffix express?
questions.explanation: The ־ְךָ ending is the 2ms attached-pronoun suffix, giving בְּרִיתְךָ 'your (ms) covenant.'

questions.prompt: The lesson notes that some prepositions, such as אַחֲרֵי, אֶל, and תַּחַת, take a special set of attached-pronoun suffixes. Which suffix set is it?
choices: The same suffix set used on plural-host nouns
The same suffix set used on singular-host nouns
No suffixes attach to these prepositions
A unique preposition-only suffix set found nowhere else
questions.explanation: These prepositions act like plural nouns, so they take the plural-host suffix set rather than the singular-host set, even though the preposition itself has no plural meaning.

questions.prompt: What person, gender, number, and meaning does the Qal Imperfect form אֶשְׁמֹר express?
questions.explanation: The אֶ- prefix marks 1cs in the Qal Imperfect, so אֶשְׁמֹר means 'I will guard.'

questions.prompt: True or false: תִּשְׁמֹר is written identically whether it means 'you (ms) will guard' or 'she will guard'; only the subject expressed elsewhere in the clause, or the discourse context, can disambiguate it.
questions.explanation: The book prints the same form תִּשְׁמֹר for both 2ms and 3fs Qal Imperfect, with no morphological distinction between them; only an explicit subject or context resolves the ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Like the Perfect conjugation, the Imperfect distinguishes real from irreal mood by word order. Which order marks the Irreal (non-real) use of the Imperfect?
choices: Word order plays no role for the Imperfect
questions.explanation: The Imperfect uses the same real/irreal word-order contrast as the Perfect: real-mood clauses keep Subject-Verb order, while irreal-mood clauses invert to Verb-Subject order.

questions.prompt: Read this clause: לֹא תִשְׁמַע אֶת־קוֹלוֹ ('do not listen to his voice'). What function does this negated Imperfect clause express?
choices: A habitual event that occurred in the past
questions.explanation: לֹא plus an Imperfect verb is the lesson's most frequent expression of the Irreal Imperfect's modal range: a categorical negative prohibition, comparable to the Decalogue's לֹא-prefixed commands.

questions.prompt: What is the Qal Infinitive of the root שמר, and what grammatical property does an Infinitive have that a Perfect or Imperfect verb does not?
choices: שָׁמוֹר; it is inflected only for gender, not person
נִשְׁמַר; it is inflected only for number, not gender
יִשְׁמֹר; it is inflected for tense and person
שְׁמֹר; it is not inflected for person, gender, or number
questions.explanation: The Qal Infinitive of שמר is שְׁמֹר; unlike the Perfect and Imperfect, Infinitives are a single uninflected form, not marked for person, gender, or number.

questions.prompt: Read this clause: הָאִישׁ הָלַךְ לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־הָעִיר ('the man went to guard the city'). What function does the infinitive phrase לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־הָעִיר express here?
choices: Purpose or result of the man's going
questions.explanation: An Infinitive with the לְ preposition typically expresses purpose or result; here it explains why the man went — in order to guard the city.

questions.prompt: An Infinitive may take an attached pronoun that expresses either its subject (the one performing the action) or its object (the one affected by it) — for example, a form glossed 'your keeping' could mean either 'you keep [something]' or '[someone] keeps you.' What determines which role the pronoun plays?
choices: Whether the Infinitive has the לְ preposition
questions.explanation: The lesson states that an attached pronoun on an Infinitive can express either its subject or its object; only the surrounding context reveals which.

questions.prompt: Which preposition(s), when placed before an Infinitive, give it a temporal meaning ('when X happened')?
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that an Infinitive with the בְּ or כְּ preposition expresses a temporal relationship, glossed as 'when X.'

questions.prompt: Both the Perfect (L21) and the Imperfect (L23) conjugations use the same word-order contrast to mark real versus irreal mood. What is that contrast?
choices: Verb-Subject order = real, Subject-Verb order = irreal
Word order never affects mood; only the וְ prefix does
Only person marking distinguishes real from irreal, not word order
Subject-Verb order = real, Verb-Subject order = irreal
questions.explanation: Both conjugations share the same rule: real-mood clauses keep basic Subject-Verb order, while irreal-mood clauses invert to Verb-Subject order.

questions.prompt: Which grammatical feature is shared by BOTH the Infinitive (L24) and the Adverbial Infinitive (L25)?
choices: Both always require an attached לְ prefix before them
Both always trigger the same Verb-Subject word order pattern
Neither is inflected for person, gender, or number
Both can only ever appear together with Qal-stem verbs
questions.explanation: Both kinds of infinitive are uninflected forms — neither changes for person, gender, or number — though they differ sharply in function and spelling.

questions.prompt: How does the Qal Adverbial Infinitive שָׁמוֹר (L25) differ in spelling and function from the Qal construct Infinitive שְׁמֹר (L24)?
choices: they are spelled in exactly the same way, letter for letter and vowel for vowel, and differ only in their overall meaning
שְׁמֹר is used only with plural subjects in every case, while שָׁמוֹר is used only with singular subjects
שָׁמוֹר has an added holem-vav and functions as an adverb paired with a finite verb, while שְׁמֹר can serve as a clause's subject or object
שָׁמוֹר freely takes attached pronouns to mark its subject or object, while שְׁמֹר never takes them at all
questions.explanation: שָׁמוֹר is spelled with a holem-vav and only functions adverbially alongside a finite verb of the same root/בִּנְיָן, while the construct Infinitive שְׁמֹר can itself serve as a clause's subject, object, or purpose phrase.

questions.prompt: In this Hebrew phrase, glossed as 'his keeping of the covenant': שָׁמְרוֹ אֶת־הַבְּרִית — what grammatical role does the attached pronoun on שָׁמְרוֹ play?
choices: The infinitive's direct object, not its subject
questions.explanation: Given the gloss 'his keeping,' the attached pronoun on the Infinitive שָׁמְרוֹ is functioning as its subject (the one doing the keeping), one of the two roles context can assign to an infinitive's attached pronoun.

questions.prompt: Read this clause: הָאִישׁ יָצָא לִדְרֹשׁ אֶת־הַמֶּלֶךְ ('the man went out to seek the king'). What does the infinitive phrase לִדְרֹשׁ אֶת־הַמֶּלֶךְ express?
choices: Purpose/result of the man's going out
The main grammatical subject of the entire sentence
A temporal clause describing when the action happened
An irreal command directed at the king himself
questions.explanation: לְ plus an Infinitive expresses purpose or result; here it explains why the man went out — in order to seek the king.

questions.prompt: True or false: like the Irreal Perfect, the Irreal Imperfect (Verb-Subject order) can also mark commands, and it most frequently does so as a negative prohibition using לֹא.
questions.explanation: The Irreal Imperfect covers the same modal range as the Irreal Perfect, but its single most frequent use is the categorical negative prohibition marked with לֹא.

questions.prompt: An attached pronoun on a noun (L22) always marks possession. On an Infinitive (L24), what determines whether an attached pronoun is functioning as its subject or its object?
questions.explanation: Unlike an attached pronoun on a noun, which always marks possession, an attached pronoun on an Infinitive may express either subject or object; only context tells which.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly converts the real-mood clause הָאִישׁ יִשְׁמֹר אֶת־הַיּוֹם ('the man will keep the day') into an Irreal Imperfect clause expressing a command, following the same word-order rule taught for the Perfect?
questions.explanation: As with the Perfect, converting to the Irreal Imperfect requires inverting to Verb-Subject order and prefixing the verb with וְ: וְיִשְׁמֹר הָאִישׁ אֶת־הַיּוֹם.

questions.prompt: Which construction pairs a finite verb with an infinitive of the identical root and בִּנְיָן for modal emphasis, rather than expressing purpose with לְ?
questions.explanation: Only the Adverbial Infinitive is paired with a finite verb of the same root and בִּנְיָן to add modal emphasis; the construct Infinitive with לְ instead marks purpose or result.

questions.prompt: Clause A: הָאִישׁ שָׁמַר אֶת־הַבְּרִית (Subject-Verb order — 'the man kept the covenant,' reporting a past event). Clause B: וְשָׁמַר הָאִישׁ אֶת־הַבְּרִית (Verb-Subject order — '[so] the man must keep the covenant,' an instruction). Which clause illustrates the Irreal use of the Perfect?
questions.explanation: Clause B inverts to Verb-Subject order and is prefixed with וְ, marking the Irreal (instruction) use of the Perfect; Clause A keeps Subject-Verb order and reports a real, completed event.

questions.prompt: How does the spelling of the Qal Adverbial Infinitive שָׁמוֹר differ from the Qal (construct) Infinitive שְׁמֹר, and how does its function differ?
choices: שָׁמוֹר adds a הּ suffix, and this form marks the grammatical subject of its clause
they are spelled completely identically and are fully interchangeable in every function
שָׁמוֹר is a special form that only ever appears within negated prohibition clauses
שָׁמוֹר adds a holem-vav and pairs adverbially with a finite verb, unlike clause-functioning שְׁמֹר
questions.explanation: שָׁמוֹר is spelled with a holem-vav, distinct from the construct Infinitive שְׁמֹר, and it functions only as an adverb modifying a finite verb of the same root and בִּנְיָן, not as a clause's subject or object.

questions.prompt: For the Adverbial Infinitive construction to add its modal nuance, what must the paired finite verb share with the infinitive?
questions.explanation: The Adverbial Infinitive is used with a finite verb of the same root and בִּנְיָן; that repetition of root and stem is what produces the modal emphasis.

questions.prompt: Read this original clause: שָׁמוֹר יִשְׁמֹר הָאִישׁ אֶת־הַבְּרִית — the finite verb יִשְׁמֹר is paired with the infinitive שָׁמוֹר of the same root and בִּנְיָן. What does the paired infinitive add to the meaning?
choices: The direct object argument of the main verb
Modal emphasis, such as certainty or intensity
A subordinate clause explaining the reason
A special marker indicating a plural subject
questions.explanation: Pairing שָׁמוֹר with יִשְׁמֹר intensifies the statement modally ('he will surely/certainly keep...'); the Adverbial Infinitive itself carries no separate grammatical role such as object or subject.

questions.prompt: The Qal Adverbial Infinitive of שמר is שָׁמוֹר, built by inserting a holem-vav into the construct-infinitive pattern שְׁמֹר. Applying that same pattern to פקד (construct infinitive פְּקֹד), which form is its Qal Adverbial Infinitive?
questions.explanation: Following the שְׁמֹר→שָׁמוֹר pattern, the construct infinitive פְּקֹד becomes the Adverbial Infinitive פָּקוֹד, with the same holem-vav inserted after the second root letter.

questions.prompt: The lesson notes that נגע ('touch') often does not take a simple noun as its object. What does it often take instead?
choices: A noun phrase marked with לְ ('to/for')
A noun phrase marked with מִן ('from')
Just an attached pronoun, never any preposition
A noun phrase marked with בְּ ('in, at, or with')
questions.explanation: Lesson 26 notes that נגע 'touch' often takes its object as a בְּ prepositional phrase rather than as a bare noun; this is a tendency for this particular verb, not an absolute rule, and object-marking generally must be memorized per verb.

questions.prompt: In Hebrew, how is a verb's direct object normally marked, according to this lesson?
choices: Always and only by attaching a preposition to the noun, with a bare direct object never permitted
Always and only by using the attached-pronoun suffix set directly on the verb itself, never any other way
Either as a simple noun (often with אֵת/אֶת if definite) or as a preposition plus noun, depending on the individual verb
Only by fixed word order in the clause, with absolutely no other marking permitted at all
questions.explanation: Objects in Hebrew may be simple nouns, but many verbs instead require a specific preposition plus noun; which pattern a verb uses must be memorized for that verb.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the clause means 'YHWH visited the man': יְהוָה פָּקַד ____.
questions.explanation: אֶת־הָאִישׁ, marked with the direct-object particle אֶת before the definite noun, is the object that פָּקַד's action affects.

questions.prompt: Which of these words introduced in Lesson 26 is a preposition rather than a noun or verb?
questions.explanation: בֵּין ('between') is the preposition introduced in this lesson's vocabulary; בּוֹא and שָׁפַט are verbs, and מִשְׁפָּט and צְדָקָה are nouns.

questions.prompt: What person, gender, number, and meaning does יִשְׁמְרוּ express?
questions.explanation: The יִ-...־וּ combination marks 3mp in the Qal Imperfect, so יִשְׁמְרוּ means 'they (mp) will guard.'

questions.prompt: תִּשְׁמֹרְנָה is written identically for which two grammatical categories in the Qal Imperfect?
questions.explanation: Like the singular 2ms/3fs syncretism, the plural form תִּשְׁמֹרְנָה is written the same for both 3fp ('they, fp, will guard') and 2fp ('you, fp, will guard'); only subject or context disambiguates.

questions.prompt: Which prefix (with no suffix) marks the 1cp ('we will guard') Qal Imperfect form?
questions.explanation: The נִ- prefix with no suffix marks 1cp in the Qal Imperfect, giving נִשְׁמֹר 'we will guard.'

questions.prompt: Convert this singular clause to its plural (3mp) counterpart: הוּא יִשְׁמֹר אֶת־הַדָּבָר ('he will guard the word').
questions.explanation: The subject pronoun becomes plural (הֵם) and the verb takes the matching 3mp Imperfect form יִשְׁמְרוּ; the other options mismatch subject and verb number, or use the wrong gender.

questions.prompt: What person, gender, number, and meaning does יִהְיֶה express?
questions.explanation: יִהְיֶה is the 3ms Qal Imperfect of הָיָה, 'he will be.'

questions.prompt: Convert הוּא יִהְיֶה ('he will be') to its 1cp counterpart ('we will be').
questions.explanation: The 1cp Qal Imperfect of הָיָה is נִהְיֶה, paired with the subject pronoun אֲנַחְנוּ, giving אֲנַחְנוּ נִהְיֶה 'we will be.'

questions.prompt: The Imperfect of הָיָה follows the same prefix/suffix pattern as regular Qal verbs. Which regular Qal Imperfect form does תִּהְיִי ('you fs will be') structurally parallel?
questions.explanation: תִּהְיִי uses the same תִּ-...־ִי pattern as the regular 2fs Qal Imperfect form תִּשְׁמְרִי.

questions.prompt: The lesson describes הָיָה as both very frequent and ___, meaning its consonants don't purely follow the שָׁמַר pattern even though its prefixes and suffixes match.
questions.explanation: הָיָה is described as frequent and irregular; while its Imperfect takes the same prefixes and suffixes as a regular verb like שָׁמַר, its own root consonants behave differently.

questions.prompt: Based on the הִ- prefix pattern taught in this lesson, what does הִמְלִיךְ represent?
choices: A passive-sounding verb form not covered in this lesson
questions.explanation: The הִ- prefix marks a Hifil Perfect; הִמְלִיךְ is the causative Hifil built on the root of מָלַךְ ('he was king'), meaning 'he made (someone) king.'

questions.prompt: What morphological marker distinguishes Piel from Hifil in the Perfect conjugation?
choices: Piel has a הִ- prefix, while Hifil has a דָּגֵשׁ in the second root consonant
Piel and Hifil are distinguished only by meaning, never by form
Piel has a דָּגֵשׁ in the second root consonant, while Hifil has a הִ- prefix
Both use the identical דָּגֵשׁ marking with no formal difference
questions.explanation: Piel is normally marked by a דָּגֵשׁ in the second root consonant (blocked by gutturals and ר), while Hifil is marked by a הִ- prefix in the Perfect.

questions.prompt: Qal מָלַךְ means 'he was king, he reigned.' Following the same Hifil causative pattern used to build הִכְבִּיד from כָּבֵד, which Hifil form built on the same root as מָלַךְ means 'he made [someone] king'?
questions.explanation: Adding the Hifil הִ- prefix and causative sense to the root מלך gives הִמְלִיךְ, 'he made [someone] king,' paralleling how כָּבֵד 'he was heavy/honored' relates to הִכְבִּיד 'he made honored.'

questions.prompt: True or false: once you know a verb's root, the meaning of its Piel or Hifil form can always be predicted automatically from the meaning of its Qal form.
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that while some Piel/Hifil meanings relate predictably to the Qal (e.g. causative or factitive senses), many are not predictable, and some roots are not even used in the Qal — so root, בִּנְיָן, and gloss must be memorized together.

questions.prompt: Which of the following Imperfect plural forms belongs to הָיָה rather than to the regular verb שָׁמַר?
questions.explanation: יִהְיוּ ('they will be') is the 3mp Qal Imperfect of the irregular verb הָיָה; the other three forms belong to the regular paradigm verb שָׁמַר.

questions.prompt: Plural Imperfect clauses (L27) distinguish real from irreal mood by word order, the same way singular Imperfect and Perfect clauses do. How does this differ from the way subordination (L30) works?
choices: Word order marks mood, while subordination instead uses dedicated words like כִּי and אֲשֶׁר
Word order instead marks subordination here, while mood itself is marked by כִּי
Both are marked only by word order
Both are marked only by conjunctions
questions.explanation: Mood (real vs. irreal) is signaled by Subject-Verb versus Verb-Subject word order across the Perfect and Imperfect conjugations, an entirely separate mechanism from clause subordination, which is instead signaled by dedicated subordinating words such as כִּי and אֲשֶׁר.

questions.prompt: Both שָׁמַר and הָיָה show a written-form syncretism between two plural persons in the Imperfect (תִּשְׁמֹרְנָה / תִּהְיֶינָה). Which two persons share an identical form in both paradigms?
questions.explanation: In both the regular and הָיָה Imperfect paradigms, the 3fp and 2fp forms are written identically (תִּשְׁמֹרְנָה, תִּהְיֶינָה); only subject or context disambiguates them.

questions.prompt: Read this clause: הָאִישׁ הִצְלִיחַ כִּי יְהוָה בֵּרַךְ אֶת־הָעָם ('the man succeeded, because YHWH blessed the people'). What relationship does כִּי mark here?
questions.explanation: כִּי here introduces the reason the man succeeded — a causal subordinate clause, matching the 'because' gloss.

questions.prompt: Read this clause: הָאֲנָשִׁים יָדְעוּ כִּי הַמֶּלֶךְ הִמְלִיךְ אֶת־בְּנוֹ ('the men knew that the king made his son king'). What relationship does כִּי mark here?
choices: A reason/cause relationship between the two clauses
An object/complement clause for the verb 'knew'
questions.explanation: כִּי here introduces what the men knew — an object/complement clause completing יָדְעוּ — not a reason for their knowing.

questions.prompt: True or false: because וְ is a coordinating conjunction, a clause introduced by וְ can never carry a contrastive ('but') or sequential ('then') sense; context supplies only simple addition.
questions.explanation: Although וְ is grammatically coordinating, the lesson notes that context often implies 'but,' 'then,' 'though,' or even restatement, so the statement is false.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a subordinating conjunction (linking a subordinate clause to a main clause), rather than a coordinating conjunction?
questions.explanation: כִּי links a subordinate (reason or complement) clause to a main clause, while וְ, אוֹ, and אֲבָל are all coordinating conjunctions that join clauses of the same type.

questions.prompt: Convert this Qal Imperfect plural form of שָׁמַר to the corresponding form of הָיָה: תִּשְׁמְרוּ ('you mp will guard') → ? ('you mp will be')
questions.explanation: The 2mp Qal Imperfect of הָיָה is תִּהְיוּ, matching the תִּ-...־וּ pattern of the regular 2mp form תִּשְׁמְרוּ.

questions.prompt: Piel is normally recognized by a דָּגֵשׁ in the second root consonant. Which class of consonants cannot take that דָּגֵשׁ, blocking the usual Piel marking?
choices: Labials such as ב and פ
Sibilants such as שׁ and ס
questions.explanation: Gutturals and ר do not accept a דָּגֵשׁ, so Piel verbs built on roots containing them lack the usual second-consonant doubling that otherwise marks the בִּנְיָן.

questions.prompt: In the clause הַמֶּלֶךְ הִמְלִיךְ אֶת־הָאִישׁ עַל־הָעָם ('the king made the man king over the people'), what is the direct object of הִמְלִיךְ?
choices: no direct object is present here
questions.explanation: אֶת־הָאִישׁ is the person the king made king — the direct object of הִמְלִיךְ; עַל־הָעָם is a separate prepositional phrase specifying what he ruled over.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a subordinate clause from a main clause, according to this lesson?
choices: A subordinate clause is one that must always come first in the sentence, before any main clause
A subordinate clause is defined as one that structurally never contains any verb whatsoever
A subordinate clause is defined as one that is always negated in some grammatical way
A subordinate clause is grammatically controlled by another clause, while a main clause can stand on its own
questions.explanation: A main clause can stand on its own; a subordinate clause is grammatically controlled by, and dependent on, another clause.

questions.prompt: Read this clause: הָאִישׁ שָׁמַר אֶת־הַבְּרִית כִּי יָדַע אֶת־יְהוָה ('the man kept the covenant, because he knew YHWH'). What relationship does כִּי mark between the two clauses here?
questions.explanation: Here כִּי introduces the reason the man kept the covenant, a causal subordinate clause; the translation 'because' makes the relationship explicit.

questions.prompt: Read this clause: הָאֲנָשִׁים יָדְעוּ כִּי אֱלֹהִים בָּרָא אֶת־הָאָרֶץ ('the men knew that God created the land'). What relationship does כִּי mark between the two clauses here?
choices: A reason/cause relationship between the clauses
An object/complement clause for the verb 'knew'
questions.explanation: Here כִּי introduces what the men knew — an object/complement clause completing the verb יָדְעוּ — rather than giving a reason; the same word כִּי can mark either relationship depending on context.

questions.prompt: Which single Hebrew word can introduce either a reason clause or an object/complement clause, with the specific relationship determined by context?
questions.explanation: כִּי is glossed 'because, when, if, that, though' and can mark a reason clause or an object/complement clause; only context reveals which relationship is meant.

questions.prompt: Lesson 31 completes the attached-pronoun paradigm with the plural-referent forms. Which suffix means "their" when the group referred to is feminine (הֵן)?
questions.explanation: The 3fp attached pronoun is ן- (written [יהֶן]- when attached to a plural-noun host), distinct from the 3mp ם-/[יהֶם]- and the other persons/numbers.

questions.prompt: Which form means "your (fp) words," attaching a plural-referent pronoun to the plural noun host דְּבָרִים?
questions.explanation: The 2fp suffix is כֶן-/[יכֶן]-, giving דִּבְרֵיכֶן "your (fp) words"; the other options attach 3ms, 1cs, and 1cp suffixes instead.

questions.prompt: The Lesson 31 chart marks some attached-pronoun forms with brackets (e.g. [יו]-) beside a plain form (ו-). What do the bracketed forms indicate?
choices: The suffix used when the noun is feminine
The suffix used when the host noun is plural
A suffix used only in poetic style
The suffix used with prepositions rather than nouns
questions.explanation: The paradigm's footnote states that bracketed forms are used when the pronoun attaches to a plural noun; the plain form attaches to a singular noun.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence שָׁמַרְנוּ אֶת־____ so it means "We guarded them (masculine)" using the object marker plus attached pronoun.
questions.explanation: The object marker takes the form אֹת- before attached pronouns, so "them" as a direct object is אֹתָם, contrasting with לָהֶם ("to/for them") and the independent pronoun הֵם.

questions.prompt: Following the pattern shown for גָּדוֹל/גְּדוֹלִים/גְּדוֹלָה/גְּדוֹלוֹת, which form is the feminine plural of the adjective צַדִּיק ("righteous")?
questions.explanation: Adjectives take the same gender/number endings as nouns: masculine plural ־ִים, feminine singular ־ָה, feminine plural ־וֹת, exactly as shown for גָּדוֹל.

questions.prompt: Biblical Hebrew has no dedicated comparative ("-er") ending on adjectives. Which strategy does Lesson 32 give for expressing comparison ("better than")?
choices: Doubling the entire adjective for extra emphasis
Adding the definite article directly to the adjective
Using the simple adjective with the preposition מִן ("than")
Using the Piel binyan of the adjective's root
questions.explanation: Comparison is expressed by pairing the plain adjective with the preposition מִן, not by any special ending.

questions.prompt: Which phrase correctly means "a great nation," with the adjective modifying the noun and agreeing in gender and number?
questions.explanation: גּוֹי is masculine singular, so its modifying adjective must also be masculine singular: גּוֹי גָּדוֹל, matching the book's own pattern אִישׁ צַדִּיק.

questions.prompt: Lesson 32 notes that superlative meaning can also be expressed with a construct (סְמִיכוּת) phrase that repeats the same noun (e.g. "holy of holies" = "most holy"). What does this construction do?
choices: Puts the noun in construct followed by its own plural absolute form to intensify it
Puts two entirely different synonyms together into a construct chain
Adds the definite article twice for emphasis
Repeats the adjective in both absolute and construct states
questions.explanation: A נסמך-סומך phrase using the same noun twice (construct singular + plural absolute) is one more way Hebrew expresses a superlative without a dedicated ending.

questions.prompt: Both adjectives (Lesson 32) and near demonstratives (Lesson 33) can follow a definite noun as modifiers, e.g. הַגּוֹי הַגָּדוֹל ("the great nation") and הַגּוֹי הַזֶּה ("this nation"). What do both attributive patterns share?
choices: Both require the noun to be plural
Both require the modifier to come strictly before the noun in the phrase
Neither modifier ever takes the article
Both the modifier and the noun carry the article and agree in gender/number
questions.explanation: Lesson 33 states demonstratives "pattern like adjectives"; both require the article on noun and modifier when the phrase is definite, and both agree in gender and number with the noun.

questions.prompt: Which correctly means "these words" (demonstrative modifying a definite plural noun), as distinct from "his words" (attached-pronoun possession)?
questions.explanation: A demonstrative modifying a definite plural noun requires the article on both: הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה; option D instead reads as the predicate "these are words."

questions.prompt: Which pair of Hebrew forms together correctly agrees with a MASCULINE PLURAL noun — one adjective form and one "far" demonstrative form?
questions.explanation: גְּדוֹלִים is the masculine plural adjective and הֵמָּה is the masculine plural far demonstrative; the other pairs use feminine and/or singular forms that do not match a masculine plural noun.

questions.prompt: True or False: Lesson 33 states that the "far" demonstrative pronouns (that/those) are identical in form to the third-person independent (subject) pronouns.
questions.explanation: הוּא, הִיא, הֵמָּה, and הֵנָּה serve double duty as both far demonstratives and third-person independent pronouns; context tells them apart.

questions.prompt: Which Hebrew word means "these" (near demonstrative, common plural)?
questions.explanation: אֵלֶּה is the single common-gender plural near demonstrative "these"; הֵמָּה is far/plural, and זֹאת/זֶה are near singular.

questions.prompt: The "far" demonstrative pronouns (that/those) are identical in spelling to which other set of pronouns taught earlier?
questions.explanation: הוּא/הִיא/הֵמָּה/הֵנָּה double as both third-person independent subject pronouns and far demonstratives; context distinguishes the two uses.

questions.prompt: Which phrase correctly means "this young man," using the demonstrative as a noun modifier (matching the pattern הַגּוֹי הַזֶּה "this nation")?
questions.explanation: As a noun modifier, the demonstrative follows a definite noun and both carry the article: הַנַּעַר הַזֶּה, matching הַגּוֹי הַזֶּה.

questions.prompt: True or False: A demonstrative pronoun can stand alone in place of a noun (a "noun substitute"), as in זֶה הַדָּבָר, "this is the word."
questions.explanation: Lesson 33 lists "noun substitute" as one of the demonstrative's uses, alongside "noun modifier" and use as a copula complement.

questions.prompt: Which correctly means "these kings," combining the near demonstrative (Lesson 33) with the plural of the segolate noun מֶלֶךְ (Lesson 34)?
questions.explanation: The masculine plural מְלָכִים takes the plural demonstrative הָאֵלֶּה with both carrying the article: הַמְּלָכִים הָאֵלֶּה; option B wrongly pairs a plural noun with the singular feminine demonstrative זֹאת.

questions.prompt: Which phrase correctly means "a great king," pairing the segolate noun מֶלֶךְ (Lesson 34) with the adjective גָּדוֹל (Lesson 32)?
questions.explanation: מֶלֶךְ is masculine singular, so its attributive adjective must match: מֶלֶךְ גָּדוֹל; option D instead reads as a predicate clause, "the king is great."

questions.prompt: סְגֹלָת nouns like מֶלֶךְ ("king") are named for a shared vowel pattern. Where does the stress fall in the singular form?
choices: On the final syllable, like most nouns
questions.explanation: סְגֹלָת nouns are defined by first-syllable stress in the singular, unlike the regular final-syllable stress of most Hebrew nouns.

questions.prompt: Which of these סְגֹלָת-pattern nouns is stressed on the FINAL syllable rather than the first, because of its feminine ending?
questions.explanation: Lesson 34 notes that forms with the feminine ־ָה ending, like מַלְכָּה and נַעֲרָה, shift stress to the final syllable, unlike the plain masculine singular forms.

questions.prompt: How do the plural forms of סְגֹלָת nouns like נֶפֶשׁ and מֶלֶךְ behave, according to Lesson 34?
choices: They always lose their final root consonant entirely
They follow the regular plural patterns, just like other nouns
They always double their middle root consonant
They can never form a plural at all, under any circumstance
questions.explanation: Lesson 34 states the plural forms of סְגֹלָת nouns are "just like other nouns" — the special first-syllable stress pattern is a singular-only feature.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct plural of נֶפֶשׁ ("life, self"), following the regular segolate plural pattern?
questions.explanation: As a feminine noun, נֶפֶשׁ takes the ־וֹת plural ending with the regular vowel shift of the base, giving נְפָשׁוֹת.

questions.prompt: Both שָׁמַרְתִּי (Qal Perfect 1cs) and וָאֶשְׁמֹר (Qal Past Narrative 1cs) can be translated "I guarded." What distinguishes their use, per Lesson 35?
choices: The Past Narrative links a clause into a literary narrative sequence with a vav-conjunction prefix, while the Perfect does not
The Perfect form is used exclusively and only for expressing negative statements, never for anything else
The Past Narrative form can never be first person
The Perfect always requires the object marker אֶת
questions.explanation: The Past Narrative is an archaic form largely restricted to literary narrative sequencing, marked by its distinct vav-conjunction prefix, unlike the ordinary Perfect.

questions.prompt: A clause with a predicate adjective, like טוֹב הַדָּבָר ("the word is good"), keeps the predicate before the definite subject, while a Past Narrative clause like וַיִּקְרָא הָאִישׁ ("the man called") also shows Verb-Subject order. What specifically triggers the Verb-Subject order in the second case?
choices: The presence of the definite article on the subject
The Past Narrative's distinct vav-plus-dagesh-forte prefix
questions.explanation: It is specifically the Past Narrative's distinctive vocalization (vav-conjunction plus dagesh forte) that triggers Verb-Subject order in that clause type.

questions.prompt: The Lesson 35 vocabulary word בֶּגֶד ("garment") follows the noun-stress pattern taught in Lesson 34. Where does its stress fall in the singular?
choices: On the final syllable, exactly like most regular nouns
On the first syllable, since it is a סְגֹלָת-pattern noun
On the article prefix, once definite
questions.explanation: בֶּגֶד has the same three-consonant, two-segol shape as מֶלֶךְ, so it is a סְגֹלָת noun stressed on the first syllable.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly combines Past Narrative word order with the object-marker-plus-attached-pronoun construction to mean "And the man called us"?
questions.explanation: The Past Narrative verb opens the clause, the subject follows, then the object marker plus attached pronoun: וַיִּקְרָא הָאִישׁ אֹתָנוּ; option C wrongly substitutes the preposition לָנוּ ("to/for us") for the direct object.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the Past Narrative form וַיִּשְׁמֹר ("he guarded") from the Imperfect יִשְׁמֹר ("he will guard")?
choices: A completely different stem vowel pattern used throughout
A special ה- suffix added at the end
The added presence of the definite object marker
A ו conjunction prefix with a dagesh forte in the next consonant
questions.explanation: In most roots the only difference between Imperfect and Past Narrative is the ו conjunction plus dagesh forte prefixed to the Past Narrative form.

questions.prompt: According to Lesson 35, in which set(s) of Past Narrative forms is the doubling (דָּגֵשׁ) of the prefix's consonant regularly absent?
choices: First-person singular and third-person Piel forms
questions.explanation: Lesson 35 notes the דָּגֵשׁ is regularly absent both in first-person singular forms (וָאֶשְׁמֹר 'I guarded') and in third-person Piel forms (וַיְקַבֵּץ 'he gathered'); no other set is mentioned as an exception.

questions.prompt: According to Lesson 35, what word-order change does a Past Narrative verb's distinctive vocalization typically trigger in its clause?
choices: The verb moves to the end of the clause
questions.explanation: The Past Narrative's distinct vowel pattern triggers Verb-Subject word order, so the verb precedes its subject.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses Past Narrative word order to say "The man guarded the garment"?
questions.explanation: The Past Narrative verb opens the clause and precedes its subject: וַיִּשְׁמֹר הָאִישׁ אֶת־הַבֶּגֶד; option D wrongly uses the plain Imperfect instead of the Past Narrative form.

questions.prompt: וַיְהִי (Lesson 36) is the Past Narrative of הָיָה. Which binyan does it belong to?
choices: A reduplicated-sounding stem not yet covered
questions.explanation: הָיָה is a Qal verb, so its Past Narrative form וַיְהִי is likewise Qal, despite its irregular-looking shape.

questions.prompt: וַיְהִי is the Past Narrative form of which verb?
questions.explanation: וַיְהִי is the extremely frequent 3ms Past Narrative form of הָיָה.

questions.prompt: Lesson 36 explains that וַיְהִי has two common functions in narrative. Besides meaning "was/became/came," what is its other frequent use?
choices: It negates the verb that immediately follows it
It marks a rhetorical question within the story
It just marks past tense at an episode's opening, with no other meaning
It converts the noun right after it into a construct form
questions.explanation: וַיְהִי frequently just marks past tense at the opening of a narrative episode ('And it was...'), without contributing further independent meaning beyond signaling the episode's start.

questions.prompt: What is the grammatical function of לֵאמֹר in a sentence like "YHWH spoke to Moses, לֵאמֹר..."?
choices: It marks and introduces the subject of the following clause entirely
It is a complementizer that introduces direct speech and is not translated
It is simply the Past Narrative form of the verb "to say"
It fully negates the main verb of speaking in the clause
questions.explanation: לֵאמֹר is a complementizer that signals direct speech is about to follow; it has no independent translation of its own.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly opens a narrative episode with וַיְהִי, meaning roughly "And it was — the man called out"?
