questions.explanation: וַיְהִי opens the episode, and the main narrative action follows as its own Past Narrative verb-subject clause: וַיְהִי וַיִּקְרָא הָאִישׁ.

questions.prompt: Which prefix marks the Nifal Perfect (e.g. נִשְׁמַר "he was guarded")?
questions.explanation: The Nifal binyan is characterized by a נ prefix in the Perfect and related non-finite forms.

questions.prompt: How is the Nifal distinguished from the Hitpael in the Imperfect, according to Lesson 37?
choices: Nifal takes a ה prefix; Hitpael takes a נ prefix
Nifal reduplicates the last root consonant; Hitpael reduplicates the first
Nifal shows a dagesh and hireq under the prefix; Hitpael shows a ת after the prefix and a dagesh
Nifal and Hitpael are identical in every conjugation
questions.explanation: In the Imperfect, Nifal doubles the first root consonant with hireq under the prefix (יִשָּׁמֵר), while Hitpael inserts ת after the prefix and doubles the second root consonant (יִתְקַבֵּץ).

questions.prompt: What marks the Hitpael Perfect, Infinitive, and command form (e.g. הִתְקַבֵּץ "he gathered together [with others]")?
choices: A מ prefix with no dagesh
A הִת prefix plus a dagesh in the second root consonant
A נ prefix plus a dagesh in the first root consonant
A ה suffix on the final syllable
questions.explanation: The Hitpael Perfect, Infinitive, and command form all show the הִת prefix together with a dagesh doubling the second root consonant.

questions.prompt: True or False: The meaning of a Nifal or Hitpael verb can usually be predicted automatically from the meaning of the same root's active (e.g. Qal or Piel) form.
questions.explanation: Lesson 37 states that in many cases the Nifal or Hitpael meaning cannot be systematically derived from the same root's active binyan and should simply be memorized.

questions.prompt: Both the Nifal binyan (e.g. נִשְׁמַר "he was guarded") and a stative Qal verb (e.g. זָקֵן "he is/was old") can describe a state. What is the key difference between them, per Lessons 37-38?
choices: Nifal is a binyan that is only ever used together with body-part nouns in absolutely every case; stative Qal is not restricted this way at all
Nifal is a derived binyan (passive/reflexive) with its own נ/dagesh marking, while stative Qal is a basic-binyan verb using a different vowel pattern
Nifal only ever occurs in the command form in every single case; stative Qal only ever occurs in the Perfect form
They are simply two completely different spellings of the exact same underlying verb form in every case
questions.explanation: Nifal is a distinct derived binyan with its own consonantal marking (often expressing passive/reflexive senses of another root), while stative Qal verbs stay in the basic Qal binyan but use a different vowel pattern from dynamic Qal verbs.

questions.prompt: Which Qal Perfect 3ms form shows the STATIVE vowel pattern, contrasted with dynamic שָׁמַר?
questions.explanation: כָּבֵד ("he is/was heavy") uses the stative Qal Perfect vowel pattern, unlike dynamic verbs such as שָׁמַר.

questions.prompt: According to Lesson 38, how do stative verbs typically differ from dynamic verbs in forming Participles?
choices: Stative verbs always form Participles in a completely special binyan reserved only for them
Stative verbs never appear in narrative at all
Stative verbs only rarely form Participles, using instead an adjective form identical to the 3ms Perfect
Stative verbs always form Participles in exactly the same way that dynamic verbs do
questions.explanation: Stative verbs rarely form one of their own; instead they use an adjective identical in form to the 3ms Perfect, such as כָּבֵד "heavy."

questions.prompt: The stative verb form כָּבֵד ("he is/was heavy") is spelled identically to which other word, according to Lesson 38?
choices: The 3fs Perfect form of the same root
questions.explanation: Lesson 38 points out that a stative verb's 3ms Perfect form doubles as its corresponding masculine singular adjective.

questions.prompt: Stative verbs express states or entrance into a state. What time range can a stative verb like זָקֵן ("be/become old") communicate, per Lesson 38?
choices: Being in, or moving into, a given state, across past, present, or future time
Only a fully completed and finished action set in the remote past
Only a direct command that is aimed at a specific group
Only a repeated, ongoing, and clearly habitual action pattern
questions.explanation: Lesson 38 explains that stative verbs can express being or becoming in a state across past, present, or future time, depending on context.

questions.prompt: The Jussive is "identical to the Imperfect" in form (Lesson 39), apart from two named exceptions. Applying this to the strong-root stative verb זָקֵן ("be old"), whose Qal Imperfect 3ms is יִזְקַן, what is its Jussive 3ms form?
questions.explanation: Since neither named exception (the 1st-person ה- ending or the Hifil/weak-verb vowel shift) applies to this strong-root Qal stative verb, its 3rd-person Jussive is simply identical to its Imperfect: יִזְקַן.

questions.prompt: The Imperative "be guarded!" (Nifal, הִשָּׁמֵר) and "guard!" (Qal, שְׁמֹר) share which restriction taught in Lesson 39?
choices: Both occur in the second person only and cannot be negated
Both require the object marker אֶת immediately after
Both must be preceded by וַיְהִי
Both are marked by a ה- ending, like the Cohortative
questions.explanation: The Imperative restriction (second person only, never negated) applies across binyanim, to Nifal הִשָּׁמֵר just as to Qal שְׁמֹר.

questions.prompt: Applying Lesson 39's rule that first-person Jussive (Cohortative) forms add ה- "in all binyanim," what would the 1cs Cohortative of the Hitpael verb הִתְקַבֵּץ ("gather together") look like, given its 1cs Imperfect is אֶתְקַבֵּץ?
questions.explanation: Adding the ה- Cohortative ending to the 1cs Imperfect אֶתְקַבֵּץ, with the expected shift of the stressed syllable, gives אֶתְקַבְּצָה, on the model of אֶשְׁמְרָה from אֶשְׁמֹר.

questions.prompt: Which Hebrew form is the Qal JUSSIVE 3ms of הָיָה, contrasted with the Past-Narrative form וַיְהִי from Lesson 36?
questions.explanation: יְהִי is the shortened Jussive shape ("let it be"), fitting Lesson 39's note that some weak roots shorten the Jussive's second-syllable vowel relative to the fuller Imperfect יִהְיֶה; the Past Narrative וַיְהִי adds the vav-plus-dagesh prefix to this same shortened base.

questions.prompt: How is a Jussive or Imperative negated, according to Lesson 39?
choices: With לֹא, same as the Imperfect
questions.explanation: Positive and negative commands/wishes use the Jussive, and the negative is formed with אַל, never with the Imperfect's לֹא.

questions.prompt: Which ending is characteristic of the first-person Jussive (Cohortative), in all binyanim, e.g. אֶשְׁמְרָה "let me guard"?
choices: A ־ִי suffix, as in the 2fs form
A ־וּ suffix, as in the 3cp form
A ־ָה suffix, added after the verb stem
A ־ֶם suffix, as in the 2mp form
questions.explanation: First-person Jussive (Cohortative) forms regularly add a ־ָה ending across all binyanim.

questions.prompt: How does Lesson 39 say the Imperative is formed from the Jussive?
choices: By adding the ה- Cohortative ending to the Jussive
By dropping the prefix from the Jussive form
By adding the object marker before the verb
By reduplicating the Jussive's final consonant
questions.explanation: The Imperative's form is identical to the Jussive minus its prefix, and it occurs only in the second person.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Imperative occurs in the second person only and can be negated with אַל.
questions.explanation: The Imperative is indeed second-person only, but Lesson 39 states it cannot be negated at all; a negative command uses the Jussive with אַל instead.

questions.prompt: The Nifal binyan (Lesson 37) is often passive or reflexive in meaning (e.g. נִשְׁמַר "he was guarded"). Why would a passive Nifal verb NOT normally take the attached-object-pronoun construction from Lesson 40 (e.g. שְׁמָרוֹ "he guarded him")?
choices: A passive verb's subject is the one acted upon, so there is no separate direct object left to attach
Nifal verbs are never conjugated in the Perfect, where the construction applies
The construction is reserved exclusively for Hitpael verbs
Attached pronouns cannot combine with any dagesh-marked prefix
questions.explanation: Because a passive verb's grammatical subject already is the one acted upon, there is no leftover direct object for an attached object pronoun to mark.

questions.prompt: Lesson 40 (p.112) gives שְׁמָרוֹ ('he guarded him', Perfect + pronoun) and יִשְׁמְרֵהוּ ('he will guard him', Imperfect + pronoun). Based only on these two printed forms, what differs about how the pronoun attaches?
choices: The Imperfect uses a different connecting vowel before the pronoun than the Perfect does
The Imperfect drops the pronoun and attaches only a bare suffix instead
The Perfect adds an extra prefix before attaching the pronoun
Both forms attach the pronoun in an identical way, with no difference at all
questions.explanation: Comparing the two printed forms, שְׁמָרוֹ links the pronoun to the Perfect stem with one connecting vowel while יִשְׁמְרֵהוּ links it to the Imperfect stem with a different one; the page does not state a broader rule beyond what these two examples show.

questions.prompt: Which of these verbs is a STATIVE, intransitive verb (Lesson 38) that would not normally take a direct-object pronoun the way שָׁמַר ("guard") does?
questions.explanation: זָקֵן ("be old") is a stative, intransitive verb with no direct object to attach as a pronoun, unlike the dynamic transitive verbs שָׁמַר, לָקַח, and קָרָא.

questions.prompt: According to p.112, which pair are BOTH given as valid ways to say 'he will guard him' (Imperfect + 3ms object pronoun)?
choices: יִשְׁמְרֵהוּ only; יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ is not a valid alternative
questions.explanation: The page gives both יִשְׁמְרֵהוּ and יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ as accepted Imperfect+pronoun forms for 'he will guard him'; שְׁמָרוֹ is the separate Perfect+pronoun form 'he guarded him,' not an Imperfect alternative.

questions.prompt: שָׁמְרוֹ ("he guarded him") attaches the 3ms object pronoun directly to a Qal Perfect verb. What construction does this replace?
choices: שָׁמַר לְ plus an entire separate preposition phrase
שָׁמַר עִם plus an entire separate preposition phrase
a completely separate independent pronoun subject
שָׁמַר אֹתוֹ, the verb plus the object marker and attached pronoun
questions.explanation: Lesson 40 shows that an attached object pronoun on the verb (שְׁמָרוֹ) can replace the fuller construction with the object marker plus attached pronoun (שָׁמַר אֹתוֹ).

questions.prompt: According to Lesson 40, which linking-vowel class connects an attached object pronoun to a Perfect verb, versus an Imperfect/Imperative/Past-Narrative verb?
choices: It's the reverse: an i-class linking vowel attaches to the Perfect, not an a-class one
Both use the same o-class vowel throughout
Perfect uses an a-class vowel; the others use an i-class vowel
Neither uses a linking vowel; the pronoun attaches directly
questions.explanation: Lesson 40 states the Perfect uses an a-class linking vowel (שְׁמָרוֹ), while Imperfect, Imperative, and Past-Narrative verbs use an i-class linking vowel (יִשְׁמְרֵהוּ).

questions.prompt: Which suffix attached to a verb means "them" (feminine plural), per the Lesson 40 chart?
questions.explanation: The verb-attached 3fp object suffix is ן-, distinct from the 3mp ם- and the 2fp כֶן-.

questions.prompt: Which correctly means "A messenger guarded him," using an attached object pronoun rather than a separate object phrase?
questions.explanation: The Perfect verb שָׁמַר plus the 3ms suffix gives שְׁמָרוֹ "he guarded him"; option B wrongly uses an independent pronoun as the object, and C wrongly uses the Imperfect.

questions.prompt: This lesson distinguishes Topic from Focus as two kinds of fronted material that can trigger word-order inversion in Biblical Hebrew. Based on the lesson's definitions, which statement correctly distinguishes them?
choices: Topic and Focus both mark the direct object of the verb, and neither affects word order.
Focus only occurs in irreal clauses, while Topic only occurs in real clauses.
Topic presents a contrast or emphasis that a listener should notice, while Focus simply tells the reader what the clause as a whole is about.
Topic directs the reader to what the clause is about, while Focus presents a contrast or emphasis and often follows a Topic.
questions.explanation: Topic answers 'what is the clause about,' while Focus adds contrast or emphasis and commonly follows a Topic element in the clause.

questions.prompt: Lesson 18 described Biblical Hebrew as a Subject-Verb language, with inversion triggered by a grammatical word (such as כִּי) at the front of a clause. Besides such a grammatical word, what else does this lesson say can trigger Subject-Verb inversion?
choices: A negated verb placed at the end of the clause.
An adjective placed immediately after the noun it modifies.
A Topic or Focus item fronted to the start of the clause.
A construct noun placed at the end of the clause.
questions.explanation: Besides a grammatical word like כִּי, a fronted Topic or Focus item also triggers inversion of the clause's basic word order.

questions.prompt: Lesson 18 established that null-copula and participial clauses are NOT inverted by grammatical words. According to this lesson, what CAN still invert such a clause from Subject-Predicate to Predicate-Subject order?
choices: A definite article attached to the predicate noun.
A Topic or Focus item, even though grammatical words cannot trigger this inversion in a null-copula clause.
A change from masculine to feminine gender agreement.
The use of a grammatically plural subject rather than a singular one throughout the clause.
questions.explanation: Null-copula and participial clauses resist inversion by grammatical words, but a Topic or Focus element can still invert them to Predicate-Subject order.

questions.prompt: Irreal clauses normally have Verb-Subject word order. According to this lesson, what happens to that order when the subject of an irreal clause is itself focused and fronted?
choices: The word order inverts back to Subject-Verb order for that clause.
The word order stays Verb-Subject, but the verb changes conjugation.
The clause becomes a null-copula clause with no verb at all.
The subject is dropped and only the verb and object remain.
questions.explanation: In irreal clauses, whose normal order is Verb-Subject, focusing and fronting the subject inverts the order back to Subject-Verb.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how the Qal Active Participle's form relates to the Qal Perfect and Qal Imperfect?
choices: It is identical in vowel pattern to the Qal Imperfect conjugation, just with different person prefixes.
It is formed by adding a מ prefix to the Qal Perfect.
It is identical in vowel pattern to the Qal Perfect.
It has its own distinct pattern (e.g., סוֹמֵד), unlike either the Qal Perfect or Qal Imperfect.
questions.explanation: The Qal Active Participle pattern must simply be memorized as its own distinct form, unlike participles in the other binyanim, which pattern after the Perfect or Imperfect.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, how does the Nifal Participle differ in form from the Nifal Perfect?
choices: The Nifal Participle adds a מ prefix that the Perfect lacks.
The Nifal Participle uses a different root consonant than the Perfect.
The Nifal Participle has a קָמֵץ in the second syllable where the Perfect has a פַּתַח.
The Nifal Participle and the Nifal Perfect are identical in every respect.
questions.explanation: The Nifal Participle pattern matches the Nifal Perfect except that its second syllable has a קָמֵץ instead of the Perfect's פַּתַח (e.g., נִשְׁמָר vs. נִשְׁמַר).

questions.prompt: This lesson states that the Piel, Hitpael, and Hifil Participles are formed on a common pattern. Which best describes it?
choices: They add a ה prefix and follow the Perfect's vowel pattern.
They add a מ prefix and mirror the vowel pattern of the Imperfect.
They add a ת suffix and follow the Perfect's vowel pattern.
They add a נ prefix and mirror the vowel pattern of the Jussive.
questions.explanation: The Piel, Hitpael, and Hifil Participles are similar to the Imperfect conjugation but with a prefixed מ in place of the Imperfect's person prefix.

questions.prompt: This lesson notes that, like Adjectives, Participles may be used substantivally (as a noun, e.g. 'the judges') or predicatively (describing an action in a clause, with its time reference derived from context). If a Participle appears with no noun it modifies and itself functions as the clause's subject noun (e.g., 'the ones guarding'), which use is this?
choices: Construct use only, not absolute state.
questions.explanation: A Participle used on its own as an agentive noun ('the ones guarding,' 'the judges') is a substantival use, distinct from its predicative use describing an action within a clause.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, what verb form typically marks the foreground (main thread) of Biblical Hebrew narrative?
questions.explanation: The main thread or foreground of narrative discourse is marked by the Past Narrative verb form, which advances the plotline.

questions.prompt: A narrator describes a character's ongoing situation or background trait -- something that does not itself advance the plot's action -- rather than reporting the next event in the storyline. According to this lesson, which verb form does the narrator typically avoid using for such background material?
questions.explanation: When material is background rather than a plot-advancing event, the narrator avoids the Past Narrative verb, since that form signals foreground action.

questions.prompt: This lesson identifies several situations in which a narrator avoids the Past Narrative verb even within a narrative text. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
choices: Reporting a subordinate clause or reported speech.
Marking the very first clause that opens the entire book.
Communicating background information that does not advance the plotline.
Reporting an event out of its actual chronological order (e.g., an earlier event mentioned after a later one).
questions.explanation: The lesson lists background information, out-of-order events, and subordinate clauses or reported speech as reasons to avoid the Past Narrative -- not simply a text's opening clause.

questions.prompt: A narrative clause reports an event that, based on the surrounding context, must have happened earlier than the event just narrated (the story has 'flashed back'). According to this lesson, which verb form would the narrator most likely use for that earlier event, instead of the Past Narrative?
questions.explanation: To report an event out of chronological sequence, the narrator avoids the Past Narrative and instead uses the Perfect, as when a preceding event is described after the fact.

questions.prompt: This lesson's summary chart groups Biblical Hebrew conjugations as Real or Irreal. Which of the following conjugations is grouped as REAL?
questions.explanation: Lesson 44's summary chart places Past Narrative in the Real category alongside Perfect and Imperfect; Jussive, Imperative, and Irreal Perfect are all grouped as Irreal.

questions.prompt: This lesson's Venn diagram shows that the Participle, though technically an adjective, overlaps in meaning with one of the finite conjugations when used predicatively. Which conjugation does it overlap with?
questions.explanation: Although the Participle is grammatically an adjective, when used predicatively its progressive/general-present sense overlaps with the Imperfect.

questions.prompt: Only two conjugations in this lesson's summary chart are used for BOTH real and irreal expressions, forming the central opposition of the whole verbal system. Which two are they?
questions.explanation: The lesson states that only the Perfect and Imperfect conjugations are used for both real and irreal expressions, making them the central opposition in the verbal system.

questions.prompt: True or False: According to this lesson's summary chart, the Biblical Hebrew verbal system shows both contrast and overlap in meaning among its conjugations, and some of those overlapping meanings can only be distinguished by something other than semantics, such as the foreground-background distinction of the Past Narrative.
questions.explanation: The lesson states this directly: as a system the conjugations show both contrast and overlap, and some overlaps (like Imperfect vs. Participle) are disambiguated by non-semantic factors such as the Past Narrative's foreground-discourse function.

questions.prompt: Lesson 43 shows that the Perfect (not just the Past Narrative) can appear in narrative when reporting an event out of chronological order, while lesson 44's summary chart classifies the Perfect as one of the 'Real' conjugations alongside the Past Narrative and Imperfect. Which statement best combines these two lessons?
choices: The Perfect is classified as Irreal, so it cannot be used in Real narrative contexts at all.
Only the Past Narrative is ever classified as Real; the Perfect is classified as Irreal instead.
The Past Narrative and Perfect are entirely unrelated conjugations that could not appear together within one single narrative passage.
Both the Past Narrative and Perfect belong to the Real category, but only the Past Narrative marks the foregrounded main thread of the story.
questions.explanation: Lesson 44 classifies both Past Narrative and Perfect as Real conjugations, while lesson 43 shows that only the Past Narrative marks foregrounded, plot-advancing events; the Perfect can still appear for background or out-of-order material.

questions.prompt: Lessons 41-45 mix syntax/discourse topics with topics that introduce new inflected paradigms. Which pair of lessons in this range introduces new inflected forms to memorize, as opposed to a purely syntactic or conceptual rule?
choices: Lesson 41 (Topic and Focus) and lesson 43 (Foreground and Background).
Lesson 43 (Foreground and Background) and lesson 44 (Verbal System Summary).
Lesson 42 (Participles) and lesson 45 (Numerals) both introduce new forms.
Lesson 41 (Topic and Focus) and lesson 44 (Verbal System Summary).
questions.explanation: Lesson 42 introduces the Participle paradigms and lesson 45 introduces the numeral paradigms; lessons 41, 43, and 44 are syntax/discourse or summary lessons that introduce no new inflected forms of their own.

questions.prompt: Lesson 44 classifies the Jussive as an Irreal conjugation, whose basic word order (per earlier lessons) is Verb-Subject. Lesson 41 explains what can invert that irreal order to Subject-Verb. Combining the two lessons, what would cause a Jussive clause to appear with Subject-Verb order instead of the expected Verb-Subject order?
choices: The verb is changed from Jussive to Imperative.
The clause is negated with לֹא instead of אַל.
The subject of the Jussive clause is focused and fronted.
The subject is dropped and replaced with a null subject.
questions.explanation: Per lesson 44, Jussive clauses are Irreal and default to Verb-Subject order; per lesson 41, fronting and focusing the subject of such an irreal clause inverts it to Subject-Verb order.

questions.prompt: Which construct-form numeral correctly fills the blank to express 'two cities,' given that עִיר / עָרִים ('city/cities') is a feminine noun? ___ עָרִים
questions.explanation: עִיר/עָרִים is feminine, so the numeral 'two' must take the construct form used with feminine nouns, שְׁתֵּי, immediately before the noun it is bound to.

questions.prompt: Lesson 42 notes that a predicative Participle's time reference is supplied by context, and lesson 43 shows the Past Narrative always marks the foreground of a story. Combining the two lessons, which statement is accurate?
choices: A Participle can describe background without one fixed tense, unlike the fixed, foreground-marking Past Narrative.
Both the Participle and Past Narrative consistently mark the foregrounded, plot-advancing events of a story.
The Participle can only be used substantivally, so it is incapable of describing any background material at all.
The Past Narrative, exactly like the Participle, draws its entire time reference from surrounding context.
questions.explanation: The Participle's temporal location is derived from context and it often supplies background description, while the Past Narrative specifically marks the foregrounded, plot-advancing main thread of a narrative and is fixed to past time.

questions.prompt: Using the Qal Active Participle of שָׁמַר as a substantival plural noun ('guards'), which numeral correctly fills the blank to express 'three guards,' given that שֹׁמְרִים is a masculine plural noun? ___ שֹׁמְרִים
questions.explanation: שֹׁמְרִים (guards) is a masculine plural participle used as a noun, so the numeral 'three' takes the form used with masculine nouns, שְׁלֹשָׁה.

questions.prompt: Suppose a narrator wants to signal that a numeral phrase like 'twelve sons' is exactly what the following stretch of narrative is about -- its Topic. According to lesson 41's account of Topic and word order, where would this Topic phrase most naturally be placed in its clause?
choices: At the very end of the clause, after the verb and subject.
It cannot be a Topic, since only single words (not numeral phrases) can function as a Topic.
At the front of the clause, in the special Topic position.
Immediately after the main verb, before the subject.
questions.explanation: Topics and Focus items are placed at the front of the clause (the 'Topic position'), a placement lesson 41 calls fronting, regardless of whether the fronted item is a single word or a longer phrase such as a numeral phrase.

questions.prompt: A background clause (not a plot-advancing event, per lesson 43) is irreal, and its subject has also been focused and fronted (per lesson 41). Since an irreal clause's normal word order is Verb-Subject, what word order would this clause most likely show?
choices: Verb-Subject order, because background status keeps this clause's word order unchanged, regardless of any fronting.
Subject-Verb order, because a fronted Focus subject flips the clause's usual pattern back, regardless of foreground or background status.
No verb at all, because background clauses cannot contain a finite verb of any kind.
Object-Verb-Subject order, a pattern neither lesson actually discusses at all.
questions.explanation: Lesson 41 states that for irreal clauses, whose normal order is Verb-Subject, focusing and fronting a subject triggers inversion back to Subject-Verb order; this fronting rule operates independently of the foreground/background distinction from lesson 43.

questions.prompt: Lesson 20 states that a construct (bound) noun cannot itself take the definite article. Lesson 45 shows that the construct forms of 2-10 (e.g., שְׁלֹשֶׁת, שְׁתֵּי) place the numeral in construct with the counted noun. Applying lesson 20's rule to this construction, where would a definite article go if the counted noun were made definite?
choices: On the counted noun itself, not on the construct-state numeral.
On the construct-state numeral, not on the counted noun.
On both the numeral and the noun simultaneously.
Nowhere -- construct-numeral phrases cannot be made definite.
questions.explanation: Since a construct-state word cannot itself take the definite article, a construct-state numeral followed by its counted noun can only be made definite by placing the article on the counted noun, exactly as with any other bound-noun phrase.

questions.prompt: Lesson 44's Venn diagram shows the predicative Participle overlapping in meaning with the Imperfect (both can express a general present or progressive sense). Despite this semantic overlap, how do the two remain grammatically distinct according to what you have learned?
choices: They are not actually distinct; the Participle simply is a form of the Imperfect.
The Imperfect can be used substantivally as a noun, while the Participle cannot.
The Participle refers only to the past tense, while the Imperfect refers only to the future tense, with no overlap at all.
The Participle is grammatically an adjective with its own binyan forms; the Imperfect is a finite verb with person/gender/number affixes.
questions.explanation: Even though their meanings can overlap when the Participle is used predicatively, the Participle remains an adjective formed on binyan-specific patterns, while the Imperfect is a finite verb conjugation marked by person/gender/number affixes.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how the numeral 'one' (אֶחָד / אַחַת) functions grammatically in this lesson?
choices: It is a noun that takes the opposite gender from the noun it modifies.
It is a noun placed in construct with the noun it modifies, like the numbers 2-10.
It is invariable and does not change for gender.
It functions as an adjective, agreeing in gender and number with the noun it modifies.
questions.explanation: Unlike 2-10, which are nouns of opposite gender to what they modify, the numeral 'one' is an adjective that agrees in gender and number with its noun.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, how do the numerals 3-10 agree in gender with the noun they modify, in contrast to 1 and 2?
choices: 3-10 appear only in the construct state, unlike 1 and 2.
3-10 agree in the same gender as the noun, exactly like 1 and 2.
3-10 take the opposite gender form from the noun they modify, unlike 1 and 2.
3-10 have no gender distinction at all, while 1 and 2 do.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that 3-10 (unlike 1 and 2) take the opposite gender form from the noun they modify -- e.g., a feminine-looking numeral form with masculine nouns.

questions.prompt: This lesson notes that some nouns stay in the singular form even when modified by a numeral greater than one (e.g., '11 year,' '11 day,' '11 man'). What does this illustrate?
choices: That numerals above ten always require the construct state.
That certain common nouns remain grammatically singular despite being modified by a numerically plural numeral.
That numerals do not agree in gender with the nouns they modify.
That such nouns must always appear as dual forms instead of ordinary plural forms in this construction.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives examples like אַחַד עָשָׂר שָׁנָה ('11 years') where the modified noun stays singular in form even though the numeral value is plural.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, how are the tens (20, 30, 40 ... 90) formed?
choices: As the plural forms of the numerals 2-9 (e.g., 20 is the plural of 2).
As the construct forms of the numerals 11-19.
By doubling the ones digit and adding the numeral 10.
As irregular forms unrelated to any other numeral in the system.
questions.explanation: The tens 20-90 are formed as the plural forms of the corresponding numerals 2-9.

questions.prompt: Lesson 46 expands the definition of Topic from lesson 41 into three levels. Which correctly lists and defines those three levels?
choices: Sentence Topic (the first word), Paragraph Topic (the last word), and Book Topic (the title).
Syntactic Topic (a special front-of-clause position), Clause Topic (what the rest of the clause is about), and Discourse Topic (what the rest of a discourse is about).
Subject Topic, Object Topic, and Predicate Topic, each corresponding to one of the three core grammatical constituents of any given clause.
Real Topic and Irreal Topic, corresponding to the Real/Irreal conjugation split.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes a Syntactic Topic (a special front-of-clause slot), a Clause Topic (what a given clause is about), and a Discourse Topic (what a larger stretch of discourse, from a clause to a multipart story, is about).

questions.prompt: A chapter repeats a certain participant as the grammatical subject in nearly every verse (only a handful of verses lack it), and the whole chapter is summarized by a single opening verse naming this participant alongside its main action. According to this lesson's analysis, what kind of Topic does this repeated participant function as, at minimum?
choices: A Discourse Topic for the chapter as a whole.
Only a Syntactic Topic, not a Clause or Discourse Topic.
An Object, not a Topic of any kind.
A Focus item, not a Topic.
questions.explanation: The lesson identifies a participant repeated as subject across nearly every verse of a chapter, and summarized in its opening verse, as functioning at minimum as that chapter's Discourse Topic.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, is it possible for the Syntactic Topic of a clause to be a different element than that clause's Discourse Topic?
choices: No -- the lesson says the Syntactic Topic must always coincide with the Discourse Topic.
No -- a clause can only have a Syntactic Topic if it altogether lacks a Discourse Topic.
Yes -- but only in clauses that contain no finite verb whatsoever.
Yes -- the lesson gives an example where they highlight two different topics.
questions.explanation: The lesson shows that while the Syntactic Topic position most often coincides with the Discourse or Clause Topic, in Genesis 1:27 the fronted phrase בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים highlights a different Clausal Topic than the passage's ongoing Discourse Topic אֱלֹהִים.

questions.prompt: In a two-clause verse, the first clause has a Discourse-Topic participant as its subject, but the second clause makes no mention of that participant at all -- instead its subject is a different noun, and the verb is a form of הָיָה. According to this lesson's method, what is the Topic of that second clause?
choices: The same Discourse Topic that the first clause had, since a lesson-46 Topic cannot change partway through a passage.
There is no Topic in a clause that uses a form of הָיָה.
The different noun that serves as the second clause's own subject -- its Clause Topic, distinct from the ongoing Discourse Topic.
The verb הָיָה itself, since verbs can serve as Topics.
questions.explanation: The lesson shows that a clause's own subject can be its Clause Topic even when a different participant serves as the passage's larger Discourse Topic -- as when a following clause shifts to a new subject with הָיָה.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, what is the basic functional difference between a disjunctive accent and a conjunctive accent?
choices: A disjunctive accent marks the formal end of an entire biblical book; a conjunctive accent marks the end of a chapter only.
A disjunctive accent makes a sense break with what follows; a conjunctive accent makes a sense connection with what follows.
A disjunctive accent only appears on verbs; a conjunctive accent only appears on nouns.
A disjunctive accent marks vowel length; a conjunctive accent marks consonant doubling.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines disjunctive accents as marking a sense break with what follows and conjunctive accents as marking a sense connection with what follows.

questions.prompt: Which pair of accents does this lesson place at Level 1, the strongest level of disjunction?
questions.explanation: Silluq (always paired with sof pasuq) and Atnah are listed as the Level 1 disjunctive accents, the strongest level, and Level 1 accents frequently lengthen the vowel of the accented syllable.

questions.prompt: This lesson discusses Isaiah 40:3, where observing the accent-marked division of the verse yields one reading of a prepositional phrase, while the Septuagint and New Testament instead read that same phrase differently. What does this example illustrate about the accents?
choices: The accents were added centuries later by New Testament-era Greek scribes and so postdate the original Hebrew text entirely.
The accents only mark musical chant, with no bearing on meaning.
The accents apply only to poetic books like Psalms, Job, and Proverbs.
The accents' sense-division can be significant for interpretation, since a different clause division yields a different reading of a verse.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses Isaiah 40:3 to show that the sense-break location marked by the accents can affect how a verse is interpreted, since the accent-based division differs from the division reflected in the Septuagint and New Testament.

questions.prompt: True or False: According to this lesson, verse divisions by the accents can be understood as a continuous dichotomy, where the strongest disjunctive accent divides the verse in half, and the next-strongest disjunctives divide each half in half again, and so on.
questions.explanation: The lesson states this directly: the strongest disjunctive accent halves the verse, and progressively weaker disjunctives keep halving each resulting section.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, what is the key difference between a complement and an adjunct?
choices: A complement is always a single word, while an adjunct is always a phrase.
An adjunct is required for the clause's basic grammaticality and meaning, while a complement is always entirely optional in every case.
A complement is limited in number and contributes to both the grammaticality and meaning of the verbal predication, while an adjunct is limitless and optional.
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable ways of describing verb modifiers.
questions.explanation: Complements are limited constituents that contribute to both the grammaticality and meaning of the verb's predication, while adjuncts are optional and limitless, adding information the author considers important without being required.

questions.prompt: This lesson shows that the same verb can carry a different sense depending on which complement set it takes -- for example, one sense taking a single prepositional complement and another sense taking both a prepositional complement and a noun complement. What does this illustrate about complements?
choices: That complements do not affect a verb's meaning, only its grammaticality.
That variation in the number and type of complements a verb takes can determine which sense of the verb is intended.
That every Hebrew verb has exactly one fixed complement set, regardless of sense.
That adjuncts, not complements, are entirely responsible for distinguishing between a verb's different senses.
questions.explanation: The lesson shows that a verb's complement set can vary with its sense -- the same verb can take one complement for one meaning and a different set of complements for another.

questions.prompt: This lesson notes that a complement can sometimes be 'null' -- left unstated but still understood -- rather than always being an overtly stated word or phrase. What earlier lesson's concept does this null-complement idea parallel?
choices: Lesson 26's discussion of prepositionally marked direct objects.
Lesson 20's rule that a construct noun cannot take the definite article.
Lesson 42's distinction between substantival and predicative Participles.
Lesson 18's earlier concept of the null subject in a clause.
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly compares a null (contextually supplied, unstated) complement to the null subject discussed back in lesson 18.

questions.prompt: A clause includes the phrase 'in the second year' describing when an event happened. According to this lesson, if this time phrase could be removed without affecting the clause's basic grammaticality (though some detail would be lost), how should it be classified?
questions.explanation: Because the time phrase is optional and its removal does not break the clause's grammaticality, it is an adjunct rather than a required complement.

questions.prompt: This lesson introduces case relations as a way of describing the syntactic role a word plays in a sentence. According to the lesson, how does English mark these case relations morphologically?
choices: English marks case on every noun with a distinct ending, just like Latin.
English preserves morphological case marking only in the personal pronouns (e.g., I/me/my).
English has no case marking of any kind, not even on pronouns.
English marks case only through word order, not through pronoun forms.
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that languages vary in how much morphological case marking they preserve, and that in English this marking survives only in the personal pronouns (subjective I/he/she..., objective me/him/her..., attributive my/his/her...).

questions.prompt: True or False: According to this lesson, Hebrew nouns carry their own morphological case endings (comparable to Latin noun declensions), and it is these endings that mark the Subjective, Objective, and Attributive case relations in a Hebrew sentence.
questions.explanation: The lesson's case relations are syntactic/semantic categories, not a Hebrew noun case-ending system. Subjective relations are read from a noun's nearness to the verb, Objective relations are often unmarked or shown lexically by אֶת/אֵת, and Attributive relations are shown by the bound (construct) noun construction -- none of these are noun-inflection case endings like Latin's.

questions.prompt: In a Hebrew clause where a Past Narrative verb is immediately followed by a subject noun, this lesson says the Subjective-case relation is normally indicated by which means?
choices: A distinct case-ending suffix that is attached directly to the subject noun itself.
The definite article attached to the subject noun.
The subject noun's syntactic nearness to the verb -- immediately before or after it.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that Subjective-case relations are normally indicated syntactically by the noun's nearness to the verb, immediately before or after it, not by any case-ending on the noun.

questions.prompt: This lesson explains that the Attributive-case relation is indicated by a particular Hebrew construction, whose bound (נִסְמָךְ) element may semantically function as the subject or object of an activity implied by the free (סוֹמֵךְ) noun, or may simply modify or express the possessor of that noun. Which construction is this?
choices: A prepositional phrase headed by עַל.
questions.explanation: Attributive-case relations are indicated by the bound noun (construct/סמיכות) construction, where the נסמך's relationship to the סומך may be subject-like, object-like, adjectival, or possessive.

questions.prompt: Lesson 49 states that case relations intersect with the valency categories of lesson 48. According to lesson 49, how do most Objective-case nouns relate to lesson 48's valency category?
choices: Most Objective-case nouns are adjuncts, not complements.
Most Objective-case nouns are complements, though lesson 49 notes some verbs take a non-objective-case complement instead.
Objective-case nouns cannot be complements or adjuncts; they form a separate valency category.
Objective-case nouns are inherently null and therefore have no valency at all.
questions.explanation: Lesson 49 states that most objective-case nouns are complements, while noting that some verbs (like יָשַׁב) instead take a non-objective-case complement, such as a locative prepositional phrase.

questions.prompt: Consider the original sentence הָעֲבָדִים יָשְׁבוּ בָּעִיר, 'The servants dwelt in the city.' Lesson 49 notes that the verb יָשַׁב is one of the verbs (per lesson 48's valency categories) that takes a non-Objective-case complement -- specifically a locative prepositional phrase. Applying this, how should בָּעִיר be classified in this sentence?
choices: As a required complement of יָשַׁב, not as an optional adjunct.
As an optional adjunct that could be removed without affecting the clause's basic sense.
As the Subjective-case relation of the clause.
As a second, prepositionally marked Objective-case relation.
questions.explanation: Lesson 49 specifically cites יָשַׁב as a verb whose complement is a locative prepositional phrase rather than an ordinary Objective-case noun; here בָּעִיר fills that required complement slot, just as בְּאֶרֶץ גֹּשֶׁן does in the lesson's own example.

questions.prompt: Lessons 46 and 49 both describe syntactic-level categories, but they classify different things. Which statement correctly distinguishes Topic (lesson 46) from Case Relations (lesson 49)?
choices: Topic describes what a clause or discourse is about, while Case Relations describe a word's syntactic role with respect to a verb or another noun.
Topic and Case Relations are simply two different names for the exact same grammatical category.
Topic only concerns individual words, while Case Relations only concern whole discourses.
Case Relations describe what a clause or discourse is about, while Topic describes the particular syntactic role that a word plays with a verb.
questions.explanation: Topic (lesson 46) organizes a clause or discourse around what it is about, at the syntactic, clausal, or discourse level, while Case Relations (lesson 49) describe the syntactic role -- subject, object, attributive, and so on -- that a word plays.

questions.prompt: A reader is trying to determine both (a) how a long verse should be broken into sense units for reading, and (b) which sense of an ambiguous verb like קָרָא is intended in one of those units. Based on lessons 47 and 50, which tools does the reader draw on for tasks (a) and (b), respectively?
choices: For (a) the reader consults case-ending morphology attached to each word in the verse, and for (b) the reader consults construct-state marking on the ambiguous word.
For (a) the reader consults the verb's binyan, and for (b) the reader consults the Topic position.
For (a) the reader consults the direct-object marker אֶת, and for (b) the reader consults the accent levels.
For (a) the reader consults the disjunctive/conjunctive accents, and for (b) the reader consults context and valency patterns (complements) to choose among the word's dictionary senses.
questions.explanation: Lesson 47 shows the accents (disjunctive vs. conjunctive, by level) mark how a verse divides into sense units, while lesson 50 shows that context and valency patterns (the complements a verb takes) help select the intended dictionary sense of an ambiguous word.

questions.prompt: Lesson 50 includes a footnote on one of its קָרָא examples, noting that the prepositional phrase לִפְנֵי ('before, in front of') in that example does not 'complete' the sense of the verb but instead specifies the location of the proclamation. Using lesson 48's terms, how should this לִפְנֵי phrase be classified?
choices: As an adjunct, since it adds optional locational information rather than completing the verb's required sense.
As a null complement, since its content is left entirely unstated within this particular clause.
questions.explanation: Lesson 50's own footnote applies lesson 48's terminology directly: the לִפְנֵי phrase is an adjunct, not a complement, because it adds optional locational information rather than being required to complete the verb's sense.

questions.prompt: True or False: According to lessons 46 and 49, a word's Discourse Topic status and its Subjective-case relation to a verb are the same thing, so any word serving as a clause's Subjective-case relation must also be that passage's Discourse Topic.
questions.explanation: These are independent categories: Discourse Topic (lesson 46) is about what a stretch of discourse is about, while the Subjective-case relation (lesson 49) is a syntactic role tied to nearness to the verb; a clause's grammatical subject need not be the passage's larger Discourse Topic, as lesson 46's own examples show.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly matches each lesson in this final five-lesson block to its primary concern?
choices: Lesson 46 = Topic; Lesson 47 = Accents; Lesson 48 = Complements/Adjuncts; Lesson 49 = Case Relations; Lesson 50 = Lexical Semantics.
Lesson 46 = Accents; Lesson 47 = Topic; Lesson 48 = Case Relations; Lesson 49 = Complements/Adjuncts; Lesson 50 = Lexical Semantics.
Lesson 46 = Lexical Semantics; Lesson 47 = Complements/Adjuncts; Lesson 48 = Accents; Lesson 49 = Topic; Lesson 50 = Case Relations.
Lesson 46 = Case Relations; Lesson 47 = Lexical Semantics; Lesson 48 = Topic; Lesson 49 = Accents; Lesson 50 = Complements/Adjuncts.
questions.explanation: In order, lessons 46-50 cover Topic, Accents, Complements and Adjuncts, Case Relations, and Lexical Semantics.

questions.prompt: A prepositional phrase built on a bound noun/סמיכות construction (an Attributive-case relation, per lesson 49) is fronted to the special Topic position at the front of its clause (per lesson 46). Can a single phrase carry both an Attributive-case relation internally and function as that clause's Syntactic Topic?
choices: No, because Attributive-case phrases can never be fronted.
No, because the Syntactic Topic position can only ever hold a bare Subjective-case noun.
No, because Case Relations and Topic are mutually exclusive categories that can never apply to one single phrase at the same time.
Yes -- lesson 46 gives exactly this kind of case, where a bound-noun (construct) prepositional phrase is fronted into the Syntactic Topic position.
questions.explanation: Case relations (how a phrase's parts relate to each other) and Topic (where information sits in the clause's information structure) are independent categories, so a bound-noun/Attributive-case phrase can indeed be fronted into the Syntactic Topic position, as lesson 46 illustrates.

questions.prompt: A verb in a clause is followed by אֶת plus a noun, then a second complement follows that. Combining lesson 49 (the direct-object marker אֶת/אֵת lexically indicates an Objective-case relation) and lesson 50 (recognizing how many verbal complements a verb takes helps identify its sense), what would finding TWO verbal complements after this verb suggest about which dictionary sense is likely intended, using קָרָא as the lesson's example?
choices: That the verb is being used with the general 'call/cry aloud' sense, which lesson 50 says usually takes only one complement.
That the verb cannot be קָרָא at all, since קָרָא never takes two complements.
That the verb is more likely being used in the 'name' or 'summon/invite' sense, which lesson 50 associates with two verbal complements.
That the second phrase must be an adjunct, since complements never occur in pairs.
questions.explanation: Lesson 50 shows that the 'name' and 'summon/invite' senses of קָרָא typically pattern with two verbal complements, so recognizing two complements (one of them marked by the Objective-case אֶת from lesson 49) points toward one of those senses rather than the single-complement senses.

questions.prompt: Both lesson 46 (Topic) and lesson 47 (Accents) discuss how a Hebrew text is organized into meaningful units, but at different levels. Which statement correctly contrasts their concerns?
choices: Topic fronting concerns which element sits at the clause's front because of what the clause is about; accents concern where pauses fall when reading the text aloud.
Topic fronting and accents are the same phenomenon studied under two different names.
Topic fronting concerns vowel length, while accents concern word order.
Accents determine which element is a clause's Discourse Topic, while Topic fronting in turn determines the strength of each accent level.
questions.explanation: Topic (lesson 46) is about clause/discourse-level information structure -- what a stretch of text is about and where that item sits syntactically -- while Accents (lesson 47) mark where sense breaks and pauses fall for reading or chanting the text aloud; they are related but distinct systems.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, what is the difference between what a dictionary/lexicon entry gives for a word and what a reader must do with that entry in an actual passage?
choices: A dictionary gives only one possible sense per word, so no further work is needed in context.
A dictionary gives decontextualized senses derived from many instances of a word's use, and the reader must judge from context which sense fits the specific passage.
A dictionary simply lists a word's senses in the exact order they happen to occur in the Hebrew Bible, and the reader just picks the first one listed.
A dictionary only records grammatical forms, not meanings, so lexical semantics is unrelated to dictionaries.
questions.explanation: Lexica contain decontextualized senses drawn from many usages of a word; the challenge in reading is assigning the correct sense to a given passage's context.

questions.prompt: This lesson distinguishes two homonyms both spelled קָרָא (Qal): one meaning 'call' and another meaning 'meet' (an alternate spelling of קָרָה). Why does the lesson raise this distinction before listing the several senses of קָרָא 'call'?
choices: Because a reader must first recognize which of two unrelated words is present before choosing among the several related senses of just one of them.
Because 'call' and 'meet' are simply two alternate spellings of the exact same word, with no real difference in meaning at all.
Because 'meet' is a later Aramaic loanword and 'call' is the only true Hebrew form.
Because the lesson wants to prove that קָרָא has no verbal complement at all.
questions.explanation: Before working out which of the several related senses of קָרָא 'call' fits a passage, a reader must first rule out the separate homonym קָרָא 'meet,' since the two are different words that happen to be spelled alike.

questions.prompt: This lesson shows that recognizing valency patterns (complements and adjuncts, from lesson 48) helps decide which sense of קָרָא is meant. According to the lesson, the senses 'name' and 'summon/invite' tend to share what valency pattern, distinguishing them from the other senses of קָרָא?
choices: They take no complement of any kind.
They take a single adjunct describing location.
They typically take exactly one verbal complement -- the thing that is announced, proclaimed, or read aloud -- unlike the other senses.
They tend to take two verbal complements -- for 'name,' the name given and the thing named; for 'summon/invite,' the person summoned and the event or person summoned to.
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that the 'name' and 'summon/invite' senses of קָרָא typically show two verbal complements, unlike the other senses, which usually have just one.

questions.prompt: This lesson compares קָרָא to the related verb צָעַק/זָעַק. According to the lesson, what distinguishes צָעַק/זָעַק from קָרָא in meaning?
choices: צָעַק/זָעַק can mean 'read aloud,' a sense קָרָא never has.
צָעַק/זָעַק is used only when the addressee being urgently petitioned is a deity, a restriction that lesson 50 says never applies to קָרָא at all.
צָעַק/זָעַק usually expresses making sounds in a distressing or alarming situation and never expresses naming or reading, while קָרָא only occasionally carries that distressed sense.
צָעַק/זָעַק and קָרָא are complete synonyms with no distinguishable senses at all.
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that צָעַק/זָעַק usually involves audible sounds made in a distressing or alarming situation and never means 'name' or 'read,' while קָרָא only occasionally shares that distressed sense -- comparing similar words like this sharpens the sense of each.
